Okay, as is tradition I return once more to shoot the shit for a few pages after catching up to the current update. This time it's the Halloween Party through Reset Six, and the progress mod isn't showing anything unfinished (one Happy Scene is still ??? but I think that might be the "Alexandria" or whatever thing mentioned upthread that I know nothing about).

General opinion summary:

I mean I get alternate timelines (alt-history fiction is a favourite of mine), I get the LiL time loop insofar as anyone does, but that whole timeline fracture and re-merge(?) was just whack.

I think we all knew who was going to be doing the murdering, Nodoka being the target was a bit of a surprise. That timeline fracture was just batshit in general, and I'm...cautiously interested in how Nodoka seems to be figuring out the temporal shenanigans on her own and going mildly insane in the process. Still don't like her after that thing with Yumi and the total lack of consequences to her after it, getting her ass kicked by Yumi aside.

If you mean the Ami/Maya scene, come on. Pocket dimension rapey lesbian bondage with a crazy bitch who may be a crazy godlike entity barely counts as NTR, especially if it's in a temporal dead-end nobody remembers after. If you mean Chika rationalizing herself into being a cuckquean, the only difference now is that she knows about it, and I'm pretty sure there's a complete psychological meltdown coming up for her.

Overall, this just felt like Blueballs: The Update. It's obviously setting up a whole lot of plot, but at the trickle speed we get this game at, it's hard not to wonder how long before any of it pays off. Financially I understand the early access model, but it's really not good for anything story-heavy. And it might help if Sel had any idea how to trim his writing. The amount of meaningless narrator rambling in the past couple updates has been worse than usual IMO.

I'm also pissed Sensei didnt even TRY to stop the murder from happening, I get non-action is his whole shtick but Akira needs to grow some balls and take things into his own hands soon.

Budoop said:
I saw some people on here saying "Nodoka sacrificed herself so I dont hate her as much" but like, that's not what happened at all.
Click to expand...
That's a narrow interpretation of what we said. Apart from DeSkel, which must have cheered for Darth Vader when A New Hope premiered, most of us had deep problems with Nodoka. Half of these was because she felt like a self-insert that had just too much knowledge and did things without consequence, and the other because of the extreme things she did. The last few updates explained and justified all of these bit by bit. Her sacrifice was just the culmination of it all.
The thing about Nodoka is that we were never able to see her in a "normal setting". From the start, we're seeing a sole warrior that by herself managed to awake and fight the simulation/reset logic without being a chosen one. Her research puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. It's possible that she's a sort of parallel to the Original Ami, in that both of them are aware of things, but Nodoka tries everything to break free (and to break everyone free), when Ami just wants to live her happy endings - this parallel might not be true though if Ami was the original chosen one, since Nodoka isn't.

It is implied that Nodoka was cursed with this burden from an early age by having to take care of her mother, that left her body behind when her mind slipped (as Akira's does) and didn't come back. Which she also did without an Akira to facilitate it, so kudos to her family. Btw, an early example of Akira facilitating slips happens with Rin after Chika's rejection, when she starts to hear clocks. Nevertheless, Nodoka can't retain her memories by divine grace, so everything she does is trial and error, and everytime they reset her, she gets fragments at most. It is implied she has gone insane from this multiple times, and from that she was able to extrapolate many rules of the resets, like the compulsion to act in a certain way by following what their past selves already did in that situation - which also extrapolates to how she knows so much about everything: it is because she has known before.

Now, when you put that into context, Nodoka is the one person acting sanely in the simulation, she understands that hurting other people is inconsequential because they're barely more than shadows, and the one thing that invokes the cycle's intervention are extreme actions. Given her fractured knowledge of things, her acts need to follow some sort of guideline which ends up being her whims (because she doesn't have the whole picture), her sexual assault on Yumi and writing the book about the simulation itself, her sexual harassment of many of the girls and even her "reveal" about Io's past all follow this logic. Those are simply the logical way to act when you know that your actions have no consequences, and that the more extreme they are, the higher the chance of getting another clue to the puzzle that might save everyone.

Further evidence of this line of thinking is displayed in the last updates, since the church, when Nodoka receives confirmation of many of her theories, she stops acting based on her whims and goes all-in into the gods, and slips and, more importantly, on letting Akira know about these things, because he is needed to go where her mother couldn't by herself. She forces Akira to slip by explaining his trauma trigger, and further explains the reset compulsion, the many layered realities, and his ability to slip others. This is what I mean when I say she puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. Nodoka is not a chosen one, she doesn't just retain her memories and have time to think about what it means. Every piece of the puzzle is fragmented and has to be fished out through a bout with madness, and yet here she is, with many more answers than the stray cat.

Another point of importance is what I mentioned regarding her mother. Nodoka lived her entire life betting on the offchance that her mother was not insane. But she didn't know that for a fact. So, for a moment, try to understand the life of a girl that had to care from her younger days for a living body without a conscience. When she finally realises, for a fact, that she was right and that she managed to figure out all of this without an Akira it is such a moment in the story.

Finally, regarding her sacrifice, Nodoka went to the roof during a reset, and Himawari tried to save her (again). Nodoka has once been saved by Himawari (presumably) when she went to recover something beyond the city's limit (probably her writings), and has been visited by Himawari (again presumably) in her dreams. It is possible that the two of them have worked, or will work together in the future, based on Shiori being how Nodoka calls her "insane" self, and Himawari calling Shiori a coworker. And yet, Himawari is unable to save her this time because Pareidolia has a mission for her.

Initially we think Pareidolia has done away with her, but actually Nodoka is one of Pareidolia's gifts scattered through the timelines. He sends Nodoka, months prior to Akira's arrival, to the Ami Happy End timeline. There, she makes contact with Sekai, the one she was researching, and is able to figure even more things out. Upon meeting Akira, our Akira, she dares to give him what she has learned thus far, that being that going to the roof is not what they're supposed to do, that she can't continue her research (presumably because that's getting the attention of the gods in a harmful way to the plan of breaking free), and, most importantly, that Ami is aware of things and a psychopath. Why is that a sacrifice? Because Nodoka knows that's going to happen. She says that his shirt will get messed up by her entrails.
Now, I still don't like Nodoka. But that's an emotional reaction to her hurting many of the characters I like. Looking at her from an objective pov, I can understand and even admire (some of) what she's done. She's been the most productive not-member of RAS, and she did all that without being chosen in any way (other than maybe Himawari's help).

That's a narrow interpretation of what we said. Apart from DeSkel, which must have cheered for Darth Vader when A New Hope premiered, most of us had deep problems with Nodoka. Half of these was because she felt like a self-insert that had just too much knowledge and did things without consequence, and the other because of the extreme things she did. The last few updates explained and justified all of these bit by bit. Her sacrifice was just the culmination of it all.
The thing about Nodoka is that we were never able to see her in a "normal setting". From the start, we're seeing a sole warrior that by herself managed to awake and fight the simulation/reset logic without being a chosen one. Her research puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. It's possible that she's a sort of parallel to the Original Ami, in that both of them are aware of things, but Nodoka tries everything to break free (and to break everyone free), when Ami just wants to live her happy endings - this parallel might not be true though if Ami was the original chosen one, since Nodoka isn't.

It is implied that Nodoka was cursed with this burden from an early age by having to take care of her mother, that left her body behind when her mind slipped (as Akira's does) and didn't come back. Which she also did without an Akira to facilitate it, so kudos to her family. Btw, an early example of Akira facilitating slips happens with Rin after Chika's rejection, when she starts to hear clocks. Nevertheless, Nodoka can't retain her memories by divine grace, so everything she does is trial and error, and everytime they reset her, she gets fragments at most. It is implied she has gone insane from this multiple times, and from that she was able to extrapolate many rules of the resets, like the compulsion to act in a certain way by following what their past selves already did in that situation - which also extrapolates to how she knows so much about everything: it is because she has known before.

Now, when you put that into context, Nodoka is the one person acting sanely in the simulation, she understands that hurting other people is inconsequential because they're barely more than shadows, and the one thing that invokes the cycle's intervention are extreme actions. Given her fractured knowledge of things, her acts need to follow some sort of guideline which ends up being her whims (because she doesn't have the whole picture), her sexual assault on Yumi and writing the book about the simulation itself, her sexual harassment of many of the girls and even her "reveal" about Io's past all follow this logic. Those are simply the logical way to act when you know that your actions have no consequences, and that the more extreme they are, the higher the chance of getting another clue to the puzzle that might save everyone.

Further evidence of this line of thinking is displayed in the last updates, since the church, when Nodoka receives confirmation of many of her theories, she stops acting based on her whims and goes all-in into the gods, and slips and, more importantly, on letting Akira know about these things, because he is needed to go where her mother couldn't by herself. She forces Akira to slip by explaining his trauma trigger, and further explains the reset compulsion, the many layered realities, and his ability to slip others. This is what I mean when I say she puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. Nodoka is not a chosen one, she doesn't just retain her memories and have time to think about what it means. Every piece of the puzzle is fragmented and has to be fished out through a bout with madness, and yet here she is, with many more answers than the stray cat.

Another point of importance is what I mentioned regarding her mother. Nodoka lived her entire life betting on the offchance that her mother was not insane. But she didn't know that for a fact. So, for a moment, try to understand the life of a girl that had to care from her younger days for a living body without a conscience. When she finally realises, for a fact, that she was right and that she managed to figure out all of this without an Akira it is such a moment in the story.

Finally, regarding her sacrifice, Nodoka went to the roof during a reset, and Himawari tried to save her (again). Nodoka has once been saved by Himawari (presumably) when she went to recover something beyond the city's limit (probably her writings), and has been visited by Himawari (again presumably) in her dreams. It is possible that the two of them have worked, or will work together in the future, based on Shiori being how Nodoka calls her "insane" self, and Himawari calling Shiori a coworker. And yet, Himawari is unable to save her this time because Pareidolia has a mission for her.

Initially we think Pareidolia has done away with her, but actually Nodoka is one of Pareidolia's gifts scattered through the timelines. He sends Nodoka, months prior to Akira's arrival, to the Ami Happy End timeline. There, she makes contact with Sekai, the one she was researching, and is able to figure even more things out. Upon meeting Akira, our Akira, she dares to give him what she has learned thus far, that being that going to the roof is not what they're supposed to do, that she can't continue her research (presumably because that's getting the attention of the gods in a harmful way to the plan of breaking free), and, most importantly, that Ami is aware of things and a psychopath. Why is that a sacrifice? Because Nodoka knows that's going to happen. She says that his shirt will get messed up by her entrails.
Now, I still don't like Nodoka. But that's an emotional reaction to her hurting many of the characters I like. Looking at her from an objective pov, I can understand and even admire (some of) what she's done. She's been the most productive not-member of RAS, and she did all that without being chosen in any way (other than maybe Himawari's help).

Nodoka does not make a leap of faith to better the lives of others at her own expense, she just gets sucked up into a reset error due to her investigations and gets shanked while taking solace in Akira and attempting to spill some beans. She's a know it all that's grasping at straws to understand the one thing she can't, she isnt going to put herself in harms way for people she doesn't even think she can harm because of the resets. I don't think it matters how much she's learnt or what she told Akira about the rooftop, she clearly didn't know what was about to happen to her and that's my point. You can put it down to semantics but she obviously had no idea what was coming to her, wasn't for the sake others, and so isn't a grandiose send off.

TLDR: I don't think her actions were out of selfless-ness, but instead personal interest.

spoilers.title: A Current Nodoka analysis
spoilers.html:
The thing about Nodoka is that we were never able to see her in a "normal setting". From the start, we're seeing a sole warrior that by herself managed to awake and fight the simulation/reset logic without being a chosen one. Her research puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. It's possible that she's a sort of parallel to the Original Ami, in that both of them are aware of things, but Nodoka tries everything to break free (and to break everyone free), when Ami just wants to live her happy endings - this parallel might not be true though if Ami was the original chosen one, since Nodoka isn't.

It is implied that Nodoka was cursed with this burden from an early age by having to take care of her mother, that left her body behind when her mind slipped (as Akira's does) and didn't come back. Which she also did without an Akira to facilitate it, so kudos to her family. Btw, an early example of Akira facilitating slips happens with Rin after Chika's rejection, when she starts to hear clocks. Nevertheless, Nodoka can't retain her memories by divine grace, so everything she does is trial and error, and everytime they reset her, she gets fragments at most. It is implied she has gone insane from this multiple times, and from that she was able to extrapolate many rules of the resets, like the compulsion to act in a certain way by following what their past selves already did in that situation - which also extrapolates to how she knows so much about everything: it is because she has known before.

Now, when you put that into context, Nodoka is the one person acting sanely in the simulation, she understands that hurting other people is inconsequential because they're barely more than shadows, and the one thing that invokes the cycle's intervention are extreme actions. Given her fractured knowledge of things, her acts need to follow some sort of guideline which ends up being her whims (because she doesn't have the whole picture), her sexual assault on Yumi and writing the book about the simulation itself, her sexual harassment of many of the girls and even her "reveal" about Io's past all follow this logic. Those are simply the logical way to act when you know that your actions have no consequences, and that the more extreme they are, the higher the chance of getting another clue to the puzzle that might save everyone.

Further evidence of this line of thinking is displayed in the last updates, since the church, when Nodoka receives confirmation of many of her theories, she stops acting based on her whims and goes all-in into the gods, and slips and, more importantly, on letting Akira know about these things, because he is needed to go where her mother couldn't by herself. She forces Akira to slip by explaining his trauma trigger, and further explains the reset compulsion, the many layered realities, and his ability to slip others. This is what I mean when I say she puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. Nodoka is not a chosen one, she doesn't just retain her memories and have time to think about what it means. Every piece of the puzzle is fragmented and has to be fished out through a bout with madness, and yet here she is, with many more answers than the stray cat.

Another point of importance is what I mentioned regarding her mother. Nodoka lived her entire life betting on the offchance that her mother was not insane. But she didn't know that for a fact. So, for a moment, try to understand the life of a girl that had to care from her younger days for a living body without a conscience. When she finally realises, for a fact, that she was right and that she managed to figure out all of this without an Akira it is such a moment in the story.

Finally, regarding her sacrifice, Nodoka went to the roof during a reset, and Himawari tried to save her (again). Nodoka has once been saved by Himawari (presumably) when she went to recover something beyond the city's limit (probably her writings), and has been visited by Himawari (again presumably) in her dreams. It is possible that the two of them have worked, or will work together in the future, based on Shiori being how Nodoka calls her "insane" self, and Himawari calling Shiori a coworker. And yet, Himawari is unable to save her this time because Pareidolia has a mission for her.

Initially we think Pareidolia has done away with her, but actually Nodoka is one of Pareidolia's gifts scattered through the timelines. He sends Nodoka, months prior to Akira's arrival, to the Ami Happy End timeline. There, she makes contact with Sekai, the one she was researching, and is able to figure even more things out. Upon meeting Akira, our Akira, she dares to give him what she has learned thus far, that being that going to the roof is not what they're supposed to do, that she can't continue her research (presumably because that's getting the attention of the gods in a harmful way to the plan of breaking free), and, most importantly, that Ami is aware of things and a psychopath. Why is that a sacrifice? Because Nodoka knows that's going to happen. She says that his shirt will get messed up by her entrails.

I can see where you're coming from. It's how everyone defines "sacrifice", which further entangles with "What was Nodoka's remaining goal when she whispered to Sensei in that timeline?" and "What really prompted Ami to kill Nodoka?".

One can view all her actions during this Halloween as "still experimenting, finally getting some results but it's something bad, but eventually accepting where her actions would lead her to like an objective scientist". This portrays Nodoka as her usual archetype, a mad scientist with actions all powered by interests in learning instead of helping others, but also with an acute mindset to accept what comes after once she flies too close to the sun. What this train of thoughts would paint Nodoka as is that her being killed in that timeline was solely due to her own pursuit in science and nothing more, regardless of whether her action "helped" Sensei and/or the time fuckery business or not. This will be her main disqualifier to claim the title "sacrifice". Or rather, she sacrificed for her own science, the kind of sacrifice we don't give a shit about. Under this lens, she at best might be considered as a martyr for Kyoko, but to say she sacrificed for Sensei would be a stretch.

On the other hand, one can also view Nodoka's final action and assume that she, at that point, was no longer pursuing science (because she finally successfully figured out something but she didn't like what she found) and really was there to help/rescue Sensei, even if that wasn't what landed her in that timeline. The key point here is to think about "Will Nodoka still die if she didn't whisper those exact words to Sensei?" and "Does getting killed right in front of Sensei a part of her goal?". If those whispered words were Ami's trigger and Nodoka knew that beforehand, this implies that Nodoka valued what her final action would bring more than her life. I just wanted to comment on a remark I saw in one of the messages and that is the notion of whether what we saw was the "real" Ami.
One of the very first lines of the entire game, spoken by an unknown narrator, is that Nothing is real.

While I don't want to take this statement literally, I'd like to reconsider the importance of figuring out which Ami, Maya, Akira or Takoyaki Man is real. How I like to interpret things is that all characters are real (or not) as they are just simply themselves. Well unless they are a shapeshifted form of Himawari I guess.

What I mean is, I don't think that timelines as such exist (even though I mentioned them plenty of times here, but I'm a hypocrite anyway). And I mean it quite literally, time is not a line from a beginning to an end. In true Kurt Vonnegut fashion (I recommend Slaughterhouse Five for anyone interested in the philosophic topic of time travel), I am a believer that time is essentially a construct invented by mankind to give structure to life, to conceptualize it. However, in fact, there is no time as such. Everything that happens is bound to happen, you cannot change it, everything exists all at once. Nothing really begins or ends, it just exists in a different form.
That is why certain characters can slip, they can instantly appear at seemingly a different point "in time" from one moment to another.

It would also explain why there have never been two instances of the same character interacting with each other (unless it wasn't them, e.g. Himawari shapeshifting). Think about how when the RAS travelled to those alternative worlds, they were not copies of their own characters, they effectively replaced them. What happened to the "original" Ayane, Akira, Yumi, Makoto from those "timelines" (for the lack of a better term)? Well, nothing, they didn't vanish. Their minds just became aware.
Which is also why I am convinced that Maya did not simply vanish into thin air and stopped existing in the Chapter 3 finale. You can hear the sound of her slipping, her conscience just traversed to somewhere else.

Anyways, enough of that philosophic mambo jambo. For all I know Selebus might not agree with my point of view whatsoever, after all he admitted that he read like five books in his life, like a true weeb Although I don't buy it, not only because he is a notorious liar, but one cannot become that good of a writer from just watching anime lol

I'm just happy to see this thread still alive and bustling during this off-time.

Okay, I've got a theory here but it's proving to be a total bitch to put into words. Time is...inconsistent in Kumon-Mi. Not in the obvious way of the loops, that's a closed timelike curve (see Groundhog Day or that one episode of Star Trek TNG), which is not what we're seeing. The looping is more like a recurring pattern of events susceptible to internal and external interference/alteration, but even then it's weird because the resets are irregular and don't go back to the same point - not every reset has the beach trip, or Dorm Wars or any of the other recurring events.

I don't think we were seeing alternate timelines, I think we were seeing previous loops. Each one placed between...I'm going to steal a term from the late Iain M. Banks here and call them "outside context problems". The events that fracture reality in a way that each subsequent loop then includes them. The first one is Sensei not running away to Kyoto with Sekai, that starts the iteration where she dies, Sensei doesn't know Ami is his biological daughter, and he goes on to meet Maya and start whatever you want to call their fucked-up relationship. Maya then exists outside the resets and doesn't lose her memories every time, and somewhere between then and the start of the game is where Ayane and Yumi end up (with the Sensei who just watches football and fucks Ami). Thousands or millions of subjective years later, Sensei "sticks" again and stops being reset with the world, I don't think we know what triggered that yet. The next fracture is Maya getting reset, which takes us up to now as of 0.45.

It's possible that she's a sort of parallel to the Original Ami, in that both of them are aware of things, but Nodoka tries everything to break free (and to break everyone free), when Ami just wants to live her happy endings - this parallel might not be true though if Ami was the original chosen one, since Nodoka isn't.

It is implied that Nodoka was cursed with this burden from an early age by having to take care of her mother, that left her body behind when her mind slipped (as Akira's does) and didn't come back. Which she also did without an Akira to facilitate it, so kudos to her family. Btw, an early example of Akira facilitating slips happens with Rin after Chika's rejection, when she starts to hear clocks. Nevertheless, Nodoka can't retain her memories by divine grace, so everything she does is trial and error, and everytime they reset her, she gets fragments at most. It is implied she has gone insane from this multiple times, and from that she was able to extrapolate many rules of the resets, like the compulsion to act in a certain way by following what their past selves already did in that situation - which also extrapolates to how she knows so much about everything: it is because she has known before.

Now, when you put that into context, Nodoka is the one person acting sanely in the simulation, she understands that hurting other people is inconsequential because they're barely more than shadows, and the one thing that invokes the cycle's intervention are extreme actions. Given her fractured knowledge of things, her acts need to follow some sort of guideline which ends up being her whims (because she doesn't have the whole picture), her sexual assault on Yumi and writing the book about the simulation itself, her sexual harassment of many of the girls and even her "reveal" about Io's past all follow this logic. Those are simply the logical way to act when you know that your actions have no consequences, and that the more extreme they are, the higher the chance of getting another clue to the puzzle that might save everyone.

Further evidence of this line of thinking is displayed in the last updates, since the church, when Nodoka receives confirmation of many of her theories, she stops acting based on her whims and goes all-in into the gods, and slips and, more importantly, on letting Akira know about these things, because he is needed to go where her mother couldn't by herself. She forces Akira to slip by explaining his trauma trigger, and further explains the reset compulsion, the many layered realities, and his ability to slip others. This is what I mean when I say she puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. Nodoka is not a chosen one, she doesn't just retain her memories and have time to think about what it means. Every piece of the puzzle is fragmented and has to be fished out through a bout with madness, and yet here she is, with many more answers than the stray cat.

Another point of importance is what I mentioned regarding her mother. Nodoka lived her entire life betting on the offchance that her mother was not insane. But she didn't know that for a fact. So, for a moment, try to understand the life of a girl that had to care from her younger days for a living body without a conscience. When she finally realises, for a fact, that she was right and that she managed to figure out all of this without an Akira it is such a moment in the story.

Finally, regarding her sacrifice, Nodoka went to the roof during a reset, and Himawari tried to save her (again). Nodoka has once been saved by Himawari (presumably) when she went to recover something beyond the city's limit (probably her writings), and has been visited by Himawari (again presumably) in her dreams. It is possible that the two of them have worked, or will work together in the future, based on Shiori being how Nodoka calls her "insane" self, and Himawari calling Shiori a coworker. And yet, Himawari is unable to save her this time because Pareidolia has a mission for her.

Initially we think Pareidolia has done away with her, but actually Nodoka is one of Pareidolia's gifts scattered through the timelines. He sends Nodoka, months prior to Akira's arrival, to the Ami Happy End timeline. There, she makes contact with Sekai, the one she was researching, and is able to figure even more things out. Upon meeting Akira, our Akira, she dares to give him what she has learned thus far, that being that going to the roof is not what they're supposed to do, that she can't continue her research (presumably because that's getting the attention of the gods in a harmful way to the plan of breaking free), and, most importantly, that Ami is aware of things and a psychopath. Why is that a sacrifice? Because Nodoka knows that's going to happen. She says that his shirt will get messed up by her entrails.
Now, I still don't like Nodoka. But that's an emotional reaction to her hurting many of the characters I like. Looking at her from an objective pov, I can understand and even admire (some of) what she's done. She's been the most productive not-member of RAS, and she did all that without being chosen in any way (other than maybe Himawari's help).

I'm quoting this post because it started the discussion and there parts of it I disagree with, but consider this a general reply. I know you're not trying to fully rehabilitate Nodoka and I agree with some of what you're saying, but I think everyone needs a reminder of just how awful she truly is.
I think you are being far too charitable in interpreting her intentions. Nodoka has straight up told us why she does all of the horrible shit that she does, and it has nothing to do with investigating the world (in contrast to her stated reasons for Nodokathon and forcing Sensei to slip). Instead she's made it really clear that she enjoys causing others to suffer and that she thinks that she's transcended conventional morality. Simply put, she is a sadist and a sociopath and makes no attempts to hide this from Sensei.
She enjoys assaulting Yumi and wants Sensei to enjoy it too.
She gets pleasure out of making other people suffer.
She doesn't care about consequences to other people as long as she gets what she wants, which in this case is the purely selfish motive of revenge.
In regards to Nodoka's research: in the alternate timeline, Yumi still beat up Nodoka despite this being a world with a completely different Sensei. I take this to mean that Nodoka Prime isn't the only Nodoka to assault Yumi, so this isn't a case of a one-off action meant to confuse the world.
She explicitly states her outlook in "Lavender". No thought of experimenting on the world, no thought of the ends justifying the means. She does terrible things and she wants Sensei to do terrible things because that is their "true nature" and she thinks giving in to your darkest desires is more justifiable than caring about others and following a moral code. I think this is really driven home by the last line - she knows she's a bad person, and she loves it.
Further expressed at the beach:
She's also a hypocrite. She claims to be doing stuff for the good of the world and those trapped in it, but she's made it clear that she'll always put herself first. She says that she loves Futaba and would do anything to avoid hurting her, but she still sleeps with Sensei behind Futaba's back and exposes Futaba's secrets in her book. When Futaba confronts her and explains how she feels betrayed, Nodoka doesn't give a shit because she's right and Futaba's wrong and that's all that really matters to her.
She starts off by disregarding Futaba's feelings because Futaba is wrong to have them.
Futaba tries to get through to her and show just how hurt she is by threatening consequences. Nodoka again ignores Futaba's side of things and only cares about what affect the threat will or won't have on Nodoka herself.
Futaba makes explicit that Nodoka is doing this all for herself and Nodoka doesn't argue.
Rather than admit that she did anything to harm Futaba, Nodoka starts making bullshit arguments for why it's really all Futaba's fault, actually. First she claims that because Futaba told her things in confidence she should be free to broadcast them to the world.
Next she tries to claim that she isn't revealing Futaba's secrets because it's a book about fictional characters. After all, she changed the character's name from Futaba to Fubiki, there no possible way anyone could see through such sophisticated obfuscation.
And as a last desperate attempt, she makes the stupidest argument of all: this is all Futaba's fault because she's the one who made the choice to read the book. Instead she could stay ignorant and happy. Just ignore the looming sword of Damocles that the book's existence represents.
Nodoka is a smart girl, there's no way that she actually believes the things that she's saying. Futaba has it right - Nodoka is trying to manipulate her into thinking that she's wrong for being hurt in the first place. It's not Futaba's feelings that she cares about, it's their possible consequences.

Even after Futaba starts crying and walks away, leaving things with their friendship possibly irrevocably damaged, Nodoka continues trying to convince her that she's wrong.
For me, it's impossible to leave this event with any conclusion other than that Nodoka possesses absolutely zero empathy for Futaba. All of her claims about people she cares about are just empty words.
I disagree strongly with the take that it's "sane" to treat other people as disposable after learning that nothing in the resets has lasting consequences. This is something that "Makoto" also says in "T is for Time", and I argued against it here. I stand by the fact that this is not a justifiable moral philosophy. It would be one thing to use the ends of escaping the cycle to justify the unpleasant means necessary to get there, but that's not what Nodoka is doing. She is incapable of recognizing that there is anything wrong with what she does. She doesn't feel the least bit of remorse. She does bad things because she wants to do them.

Nodoka represents the dark side of how one could react to learning that nothing is real and actions are transitory. She's a foil for Sensei, who does bad things but knows that they're wrong and wants to be a better person. Nodoka illustrates what he could be if he truly stopped caring and suppressed the last vestiges of his conscience. The alternative view that actions still matter is explored (with variations) through all of the other characters who know about the resets. Most obviously by Maya Prime, who despite being an inherently selfish person who has watched countless versions of her friends come and go still can't help but see them as people.

...
You could argue that this is a weakness of Maya's and that Nodoka has the strength to put emotions aside and approach the world from a detached and purely logical viewpoint. My reading is the opposite: Maya has shown strength in being able to maintain her humanity in a meaningless world. A central theme of LiL is that the notion of "real" and "unreal" is a false dichotomy and that true reality is determined by how people perceive things. If the world is real in the minds of its residents, then it's just as real as the world outside the simulation. If Nodoka's actions are real to those forced to experience them, then they matter just as much as if they had lasting consequences. After all, this is a game about Lessons in Love, not Lessons in Logic.
Okay, that's enough rambling about Nodoka as a person. I actually think all of the stuff that I've talked about are strengths of Nodoka as a character. Any good story needs bad people, and I enjoy how she's bad in different ways than Sensei and that's used to explore the game's themes. I also do like how she has been humanized a bit in recent updates, I just think we need to be careful not to let that overshadow everything that we've learned about her previously.

To finish things off, I do want to complain about the stuff that I still truly dislike about Nodoka's characterization: her genius and her "research".

Maybe it's just me, but I still find it impossible to be impressed by Nodoka's ability to "figure things out". We're never actual shown her process for learning anything (with one partial exception I'll talk about below), she just goes from not knowing things to knowing things whenever it's convenient for the story, and we still haven't been presented with any logical mechanism for how this happens. Here's what we've learned about her research:
  1. She forces people to confront new situations, the weirder the better, in order to observe how they react and to "confuse time" whatever that's supposed to actually accomplish.
  2. She's able to build up her research across resets through a combination of hidden journals and an ability to receive thoughts and/or memories directly from her past selves during her manic episodes.
The second point explains how she's able to retain knowledge, not how she gets it in the first place. The first point could explain how she seems to know everything about the game's characters and can predict how they'll react to her manipulation. (Though recently she's sucked at that, given the book plot with Futaba and the reveal with Io. There's also the issue that past Nodokas might have never met most of these people since according to Maya Prime she never joined the class before, but there's several possible explanations that get around that.) What it doesn't explain is how she could have learned anything about the world or anything supernatural.

It's fine for Nodoka's knowledge to be left mysterious. This is a game full of secrets and slow reveals. What I find infuriating is the story's insinuation that we should regard Nodoka as a super-genius who is so much better than everyone else because she solved mysteries using clues that no one else possessed, especially the reader.

One example to prove my point: we can almost see how a genius would have figured out Akira's relationship with Sekai. She heard Ami's poems on the beach and recognized their similarities to the Girl Who Cannot Breathe, which clued her in that TGWCB was Ami's mother. By reading TGWCB's poems and comparing them to what she knows about Akira's trauma, she figures out that he was "Boy" and was sexually abused. But where this falls apart is that she can't possibly have figured out from these anonymous poems that Sekai called him "Aki-kun", much less that this is a trigger for slipping. She also can't know this from trial and error in previous resets because both Akira's real name and the Akira+Sekai relationship were completely new to her when she learned them in this cycle.

Where could she have learned this? I see a few possibilities:
  • Divine revelation, most likely from Sekai herself.
  • Her mom's writings somehow talk about Akira and Sekai, maybe in Terminal 22. I think it's unlikely her mom would have known this much about their relationship, though.
  • She has access to another source of information that is completely hidden from the reader. I have a suspicion that her mom had some unpublished writings by Sekai (journals?) in her collection.
In any of these three cases, though, the information comes from an external source. Maybe she had to connect some dots, but as far as the reader knows she could have been straight up told everything.

So there's one thing that Nodoka might as well only know through divine revelation from the reader's perspective, and it's far from the only one. As long as she's allowed by the story to "just know things" why should we give her any credit for it?

It is implied she has gone insane from this multiple times, and from that she was able to extrapolate many rules of the resets, like the compulsion to act in a certain way by following what their past selves already did in that situation - which also extrapolates to how she knows so much about everything: it is because she has known before.

Now, when you put that into context, Nodoka is the one person acting sanely in the simulation, she understands that hurting other people is inconsequential because they're barely more than shadows, and the one thing that invokes the cycle's intervention are extreme actions. Given her fractured knowledge of things, her acts need to follow some sort of guideline which ends up being her whims (because she doesn't have the whole picture), her sexual assault on Yumi and writing the book about the simulation itself, her sexual harassment of many of the girls and even her "reveal" about Io's past all follow this logic. Those are simply the logical way to act when you know that your actions have no consequences, and that the more extreme they are, the higher the chance of getting another clue to the puzzle that might save everyone.

Further evidence of this line of thinking is displayed in the last updates, since the church, when Nodoka receives confirmation of many of her theories, she stops acting based on her whims and goes all-in into the gods, and slips and, more importantly, on letting Akira know about these things, because he is needed to go where her mother couldn't by herself. She forces Akira to slip by explaining his trauma trigger, and further explains the reset compulsion, the many layered realities, and his ability to slip others. This is what I mean when I say she puts everyone to shame, most of all Maya. Nodoka is not a chosen one, she doesn't just retain her memories and have time to think about what it means. Every piece of the puzzle is fragmented and has to be fished out through a bout with madness, and yet here she is, with many more answers than the stray cat.

Another point of importance is what I mentioned regarding her mother. Nodoka lived her entire life betting on the offchance that her mother was not insane. But she didn't know that for a fact. So, for a moment, try to understand the life of a girl that had to care from her younger days for a living body without a conscience. When she finally realises, for a fact, that she was right and that she managed to figure out all of this without an Akira it is such a moment in the story.

Finally, regarding her sacrifice, Nodoka went to the roof during a reset, and Himawari tried to save her (again). Nodoka has once been saved by Himawari (presumably) when she went to recover something beyond the city's limit (probably her writings), and has been visited by Himawari (again presumably) in her dreams. It is possible that the two of them have worked, or will work together in the future, based on Shiori being how Nodoka calls her "insane" self, and Himawari calling Shiori a coworker. And yet, Himawari is unable to save her this time because Pareidolia has a mission for her.

Initially we think Pareidolia has done away with her, but actually Nodoka is one of Pareidolia's gifts scattered through the timelines. He sends Nodoka, months prior to Akira's arrival, to the Ami Happy End timeline. There, she makes contact with Sekai, the one she was researching, and is able to figure even more things out. Upon meeting Akira, our Akira, she dares to give him what she has learned thus far, that being that going to the roof is not what they're supposed to do, that she can't continue her research (presumably because that's getting the attention of the gods in a harmful way to the plan of breaking free), and, most importantly, that Ami is aware of things and a psychopath. Why is that a sacrifice? Because Nodoka knows that's going to happen. She says that his shirt will get messed up by her entrails.

spoilers.title: Nodoka's actions and intentions
spoilers.html:
I think you are being far too charitable in interpreting her intentions. Nodoka has straight up told us why she does all of the horrible shit that she does, and it has nothing to do with investigating the world (in contrast to her stated reasons for Nodokathon and forcing Sensei to slip). Instead she's made it really clear that she enjoys causing others to suffer and that she thinks that she's transcended conventional morality. Simply put, she is a sadist and a sociopath and makes no attempts to hide this from Sensei.
She enjoys assaulting Yumi and wants Sensei to enjoy it too.
She gets pleasure out of making other people suffer.
She doesn't care about consequences to other people as long as she gets what she wants, which in this case is the purely selfish motive of revenge.
In regards to Nodoka's research: in the alternate timeline, Yumi still beat up Nodoka despite this being a world with a completely different Sensei. I take this to mean that Nodoka Prime isn't the only Nodoka to assault Yumi, so this isn't a case of a one-off action meant to confuse the world.
She explicitly states her outlook in "Lavender". No thought of experimenting on the world, no thought of the ends justifying the means. She does terrible things and she wants Sensei to do terrible things because that is their "true nature" and she thinks giving in to your darkest desires is more justifiable than caring about others and following a moral code. I think this is really driven home by the last line - she knows she's a bad person, and she loves it.
Further expressed at the beach:
She's also a hypocrite. She claims to be doing stuff for the good of the world and those trapped in it, but she's made it clear that she'll always put herself first. She says that she loves Futaba and would do anything to avoid hurting her, but she still sleeps with Sensei behind Futaba's back and exposes Futaba's secrets in her book. When Futaba confronts her and explains how she feels betrayed, Nodoka doesn't give a shit because she's right and Futaba's wrong and that's all that really matters to her.
She starts off by disregarding Futaba's feelings because Futaba is wrong to have them.
Futaba tries to get through to her and show just how hurt she is by threatening consequences. Nodoka again ignores Futaba's side of things and only cares about what affect the threat will or won't have on Nodoka herself.
Futaba makes explicit that Nodoka is doing this all for herself and Nodoka doesn't argue.
Rather than admit that she did anything to harm Futaba, Nodoka starts making bullshit arguments for why it's really all Futaba's fault, actually. First she claims that because Futaba told her things in confidence she should be free to broadcast them to the world.
Next she tries to claim that she isn't revealing Futaba's secrets because it's a book about fictional characters. After all, she changed the character's name from Futaba to Fubiki, there no possible way anyone could see through such sophisticated obfuscation.
And as a last desperate attempt, she makes the stupidest argument of all: this is all Futaba's fault because she's the one who made the choice to read the book. Instead she could stay ignorant and happy. Just ignore the looming sword of Damocles that the book's existence represents.
Nodoka is a smart girl, there's no way that she actually believes the things that she's saying. Futaba has it right - Nodoka is trying to manipulate her into thinking that she's wrong for being hurt in the first place. It's not Futaba's feelings that she cares about, it's their possible consequences.

Even after Futaba starts crying and walks away, leaving things with their friendship possibly irrevocably damaged, Nodoka continues trying to convince her that she's wrong.
For me, it's impossible to leave this event with any conclusion other than that Nodoka possesses absolutely zero empathy for Futaba. All of her claims about people she cares about are just empty words.

spoilers.title: reset morality
spoilers.html:
I disagree strongly with the take that it's "sane" to treat other people as disposable after learning that nothing in the resets has lasting consequences. This is something that "Makoto" also says in "T is for Time", and I argued against it here. I stand by the fact that this is not a justifiable moral philosophy. It would be one thing to use the ends of escaping the cycle to justify the unpleasant means necessary to get there, but that's not what Nodoka is doing. She is incapable of recognizing that there is anything wrong with what she does. She doesn't feel the least bit of remorse. She does bad things because she wants to do them.

Nodoka represents the dark side of how one could react to learning that nothing is real and actions are transitory. She's a foil for Sensei, who does bad things but knows that they're wrong and wants to be a better person. Nodoka illustrates what he could be if he truly stopped caring and suppressed the last vestiges of his conscience. The alternative view that actions still matter is explored (with variations) through all of the other characters who know about the resets. Most obviously by Maya Prime, who despite being an inherently selfish person who has watched countless versions of her friends come and go still can't help but see them as people.

...
You could argue that this is a weakness of Maya's and that Nodoka has the strength to put emotions aside and approach the world from a detached and purely logical viewpoint. My reading is the opposite: Maya has shown strength in being able to maintain her humanity in a meaningless world. A central theme of LiL is that the notion of "real" and "unreal" is a false dichotomy and that true reality is determined by how people perceive things. If the world is real in the minds of its residents, then it's just as real as the world outside the simulation. If Nodoka's actions are real to those forced to experience them, then they matter just as much as if they had lasting consequences. After all, this is a game about Lessons in Love, not Lessons in Logic.

spoilers.title: Nodoka as a character
spoilers.html:
Okay, that's enough rambling about Nodoka as a person. I actually think all of the stuff that I've talked about are strengths of Nodoka as a character. Any good story needs bad people, and I enjoy how she's bad in different ways than Sensei and that's used to explore the game's themes. I also do like how she has been humanized a bit in recent updates, I just think we need to be careful not to let that overshadow everything that we've learned about her previously.

To finish things off, I do want to complain about the stuff that I still truly dislike about Nodoka's characterization: her genius and her "research".

Maybe it's just me, but I still find it impossible to be impressed by Nodoka's ability to "figure things out". We're never actual shown her process for learning anything (with one partial exception I'll talk about below), she just goes from not knowing things to knowing things whenever it's convenient for the story, and we still haven't been presented with any logical mechanism for how this happens. Here's what we've learned about her research:
  1. She forces people to confront new situations, the weirder the better, in order to observe how they react and to "confuse time" whatever that's supposed to actually accomplish.
  2. She's able to build up her research across resets through a combination of hidden journals and an ability to receive thoughts and/or memories directly from her past selves during her manic episodes.
The second point explains how she's able to retain knowledge, not how she gets it in the first place. The first point could explain how she seems to know everything about the game's characters and can predict how they'll react to her manipulation. (Though recently she's sucked at that, given the book plot with Futaba and the reveal with Io. There's also the issue that past Nodokas might have never met most of these people since according to Maya Prime she never joined the class before, but there's several possible explanations that get around that.) What it doesn't explain is how she could have learned anything about the world or anything supernatural.

It's fine for Nodoka's knowledge to be left mysterious. This is a game full of secrets and slow reveals. What I find infuriating is the story's insinuation that we should regard Nodoka as a super-genius who is so much better than everyone else because she solved mysteries using clues that no one else possessed, especially the reader.

One example to prove my point: we can almost see how a genius would have figured out Akira's relationship with Sekai. She heard Ami's poems on the beach and recognized their similarities to the Girl Who Cannot Breathe, which clued her in that TGWCB was Ami's mother. By reading TGWCB's poems and comparing them to what she knows about Akira's trauma, she figures out that he was "Boy" and was sexually abused. But where this falls apart is that she can't possibly have figured out from these anonymous poems that Sekai called him "Aki-kun", much less that this is a trigger for slipping. She also can't know this from trial and error in previous resets because both Akira's real name and the Akira+Sekai relationship were completely new to her when she learned them in this cycle.

Where could she have learned this? I see a few possibilities:
  • Divine revelation, most likely from Sekai herself.
  • Her mom's writings somehow talk about Akira and Sekai, maybe in Terminal 22. I think it's unlikely her mom would have known this much about their relationship, though.
  • She has access to another source of information that is completely hidden from the reader. I have a suspicion that her mom had some unpublished writings by Sekai (journals?) in her collection.
In any of these three cases, though, the information comes from an external source. Maybe she had to connect some dots, but as far as the reader knows she could have been straight up told everything.

So there's one thing that Nodoka might as well only know through divine revelation from the reader's perspective, and it's far from the only one. As long as she's allowed by the story to "just know things" why should we give her any credit for it?

spoilers.title: reset morality
spoilers.html:
I disagree strongly with the take that it's "sane" to treat other people as disposable after learning that nothing in the resets has lasting consequences. This is something that "Makoto" also says in "T is for Time", and I argued against it here. I stand by the fact that this is not a justifiable moral philosophy. It would be one thing to use the ends of escaping the cycle to justify the unpleasant means necessary to get there, but that's not what Nodoka is doing. She is incapable of recognizing that there is anything wrong with what she does. She doesn't feel the least bit of remorse. She does bad things because she wants to do them.

Nodoka represents the dark side of how one could react to learning that nothing is real and actions are transitory. She's a foil for Sensei, who does bad things but knows that they're wrong and wants to be a better person. Nodoka illustrates what he could be if he truly stopped caring and suppressed the last vestiges of his conscience. The alternative view that actions still matter is explored (with variations) through all of the other characters who know about the resets. Most obviously by Maya Prime, who despite being an inherently selfish person who has watched countless versions of her friends come and go still can't help but see them as people.
View attachment 4273529
...
View attachment 4273530 View attachment 4273531 View attachment 4273532 View attachment 4273533
You could argue that this is a weakness of Maya's and that Nodoka has the strength to put emotions aside and approach the world from a detached and purely logical viewpoint. My reading is the opposite: Maya has shown strength in being able to maintain her humanity in a meaningless world. A central theme of LiL is that the notion of "real" and "unreal" is a false dichotomy and that true reality is determined by how people perceive things. If the world is real in the minds of its residents, then it's just as real as the world outside the simulation. If Nodoka's actions are real to those forced to experience them, then they matter just as much as if they had lasting consequences. After all, this is a game about Lessons in Love, not Lessons in Logic.

spoilers.title: Nodoka as a character
spoilers.html:
Okay, that's enough rambling about Nodoka as a person. I actually think all of the stuff that I've talked about are strengths of Nodoka as a character. Any good story needs bad people, and I enjoy how she's bad in different ways than Sensei and that's used to explore the game's themes. I also do like how she has been humanized a bit in recent updates, I just think we need to be careful not to let that overshadow everything that we've learned about her previously.

To finish things off, I do want to complain about the stuff that I still truly dislike about Nodoka's characterization: her genius and her "research".

Maybe it's just me, but I still find it impossible to be impressed by Nodoka's ability to "figure things out". We're never actual shown her process for learning anything (with one partial exception I'll talk about below), she just goes from not knowing things to knowing things whenever it's convenient for the story, and we still haven't been presented with any logical mechanism for how this happens. Here's what we've learned about her research:
  1. She forces people to confront new situations, the weirder the better, in order to observe how they react and to "confuse time" whatever that's supposed to actually accomplish.
  2. She's able to build up her research across resets through a combination of hidden journals and an ability to receive thoughts and/or memories directly from her past selves during her manic episodes.
The second point explains how she's able to retain knowledge, not how she gets it in the first place. The first point could explain how she seems to know everything about the game's characters and can predict how they'll react to her manipulation. (Though recently she's sucked at that, given the book plot with Futaba and the reveal with Io. There's also the issue that past Nodokas might have never met most of these people since according to Maya Prime she never joined the class before, but there's several possible explanations that get around that.) What it doesn't explain is how she could have learned anything about the world or anything supernatural.

It's fine for Nodoka's knowledge to be left mysterious. This is a game full of secrets and slow reveals. What I find infuriating is the story's insinuation that we should regard Nodoka as a super-genius who is so much better than everyone else because she solved mysteries using clues that no one else possessed, especially the reader.

One example to prove my point: we can almost see how a genius would have figured out Akira's relationship with Sekai. She heard Ami's poems on the beach and recognized their similarities to the Girl Who Cannot Breathe, which clued her in that TGWCB was Ami's mother. By reading TGWCB's poems and comparing them to what she knows about Akira's trauma, she figures out that he was "Boy" and was sexually abused. But where this falls apart is that she can't possibly have figured out from these anonymous poems that Sekai called him "Aki-kun", much less that this is a trigger for slipping. She also can't know this from trial and error in previous resets because both Akira's real name and the Akira+Sekai relationship were completely new to her when she learned them in this cycle.

Where could she have learned this? I see a few possibilities:
  • Divine revelation, most likely from Sekai herself.
  • Her mom's writings somehow talk about Akira and Sekai, maybe in Terminal 22. I think it's unlikely her mom would have known this much about their relationship, though.
  • She has access to another source of information that is completely hidden from the reader. I have a suspicion that her mom had some unpublished writings by Sekai (journals?) in her collection.
In any of these three cases, though, the information comes from an external source. Maybe she had to connect some dots, but as far as the reader knows she could have been straight up told everything.

So there's one thing that Nodoka might as well only know through divine revelation from the reader's perspective, and it's far from the only one. As long as she's allowed by the story to "just know things" why should we give her any credit for it?

For me, it's impossible to leave this event with any conclusion other than that Nodoka possesses absolutely zero empathy for Futaba. All of her claims about people she cares about are just empty words.
I disagree strongly with the take that it's "sane" to treat other people as disposable after learning that nothing in the resets has lasting consequences. This is something that "Makoto" also says in "T is for Time", and I argued against it here. I stand by the fact that this is not a justifiable moral philosophy. It would be one thing to use the ends of escaping the cycle to justify the unpleasant means necessary to get there, but that's not what Nodoka is doing. She is incapable of recognizing that there is anything wrong with what she does. She doesn't feel the least bit of remorse. She does bad things because she wants to do them.

Nodoka represents the dark side of how one could react to learning that nothing is real and actions are transitory. She's a foil for Sensei, who does bad things but knows that they're wrong and wants to be a better person. Nodoka illustrates what he could be if he truly stopped caring and suppressed the last vestiges of his conscience. The alternative view that actions still matter is explored (with variations) through all of the other characters who know about the resets. Most obviously by Maya Prime, who despite being an inherently selfish person who has watched countless versions of her friends come and go still can't help but see them as people.

View attachment 4273530 View attachment 4273531 View attachment 4273532 View attachment 4273533
You could argue that this is a weakness of Maya's and that Nodoka has the strength to put emotions aside and approach the world from a detached and purely logical viewpoint. My reading is the opposite: Maya has shown strength in being able to maintain her humanity in a meaningless world. A central theme of LiL is that the notion of "real" and "unreal" is a false dichotomy and that true reality is determined by how people perceive things. If the world is real in the minds of its residents, then it's just as real as the world outside the simulation. If Nodoka's actions are real to those forced to experience them, then they matter just as much as if they had lasting consequences. After all, this is a game about Lessons in Love, not Lessons in Logic.
Okay, that's enough rambling about Nodoka as a person. I actually think all of the stuff that I've talked about are strengths of Nodoka as a character. Any good story needs bad people, and I enjoy how she's bad in different ways than Sensei and that's used to explore the game's themes. I also do like how she has been humanized a bit in recent updates, I just think we need to be careful not to let that overshadow everything that we've learned about her previously.

To finish things off, I do want to complain about the stuff that I still truly dislike about Nodoka's characterization: her genius and her "research".

Maybe it's just me, but I still find it impossible to be impressed by Nodoka's ability to "figure things out". We're never actual shown her process for learning anything (with one partial exception I'll talk about below), she just goes from not knowing things to knowing things whenever it's convenient for the story, and we still haven't been presented with any logical mechanism for how this happens. Here's what we've learned about her research:
  1. She forces people to confront new situations, the weirder the better, in order to observe how they react and to "confuse time" whatever that's supposed to actually accomplish.
  2. She's able to build up her research across resets through a combination of hidden journals and an ability to receive thoughts and/or memories directly from her past selves during her manic episodes.
The second point explains how she's able to retain knowledge, not how she gets it in the first place. The first point could explain how she seems to know everything about the game's characters and can predict how they'll react to her manipulation. (Though recently she's sucked at that, given the book plot with Futaba and the reveal with Io. There's also the issue that past Nodokas might have never met most of these people since according to Maya Prime she never joined the class before, but there's several possible explanations that get around that.) What it doesn't explain is how she could have learned anything about the world or anything supernatural.

It's fine for Nodoka's knowledge to be left mysterious. This is a game full of secrets and slow reveals. What I find infuriating is the story's insinuation that we should regard Nodoka as a super-genius who is so much better than everyone else because she solved mysteries using clues that no one else possessed, especially the reader.

One example to prove my point: we can almost see how a genius would have figured out Akira's relationship with Sekai. She heard Ami's poems on the beach and recognized their similarities to the Girl Who Cannot Breathe, which clued her in that TGWCB was Ami's mother. By reading TGWCB's poems and comparing them to what she knows about Akira's trauma, she figures out that he was "Boy" and was sexually abused. But where this falls apart is that she can't possibly have figured out from these anonymous poems that Sekai called him "Aki-kun", much less that this is a trigger for slipping. She also can't know this from trial and error in previous resets because both Akira's real name and the Akira+Sekai relationship were completely new to her when she learned them in this cycle.

Where could she have learned this? I see a few possibilities:
  • Divine revelation, most likely from Sekai herself.
  • Her mom's writings somehow talk about Akira and Sekai, maybe in Terminal 22. I think it's unlikely her mom would have known this much about their relationship, though.
  • She has access to another source of information that is completely hidden from the reader. I have a suspicion that her mom had some unpublished writings by Sekai (journals?) in her collection.
In any of these three cases, though, the information comes from an external source. Maybe she had to connect some dots, but as far as the reader knows she could have been straight up told everything.

So there's one thing that Nodoka might as well only know through divine revelation from the reader's perspective, and it's far from the only one. As long as she's allowed by the story to "just know things" why should we give her any credit for it?

spoilers.title: reset morality
spoilers.html:
I disagree strongly with the take that it's "sane" to treat other people as disposable after learning that nothing in the resets has lasting consequences. This is something that "Makoto" also says in "T is for Time", and I argued against it here. I stand by the fact that this is not a justifiable moral philosophy. It would be one thing to use the ends of escaping the cycle to justify the unpleasant means necessary to get there, but that's not what Nodoka is doing. She is incapable of recognizing that there is anything wrong with what she does. She doesn't feel the least bit of remorse. She does bad things because she wants to do them.

Nodoka represents the dark side of how one could react to learning that nothing is real and actions are transitory. She's a foil for Sensei, who does bad things but knows that they're wrong and wants to be a better person. Nodoka illustrates what he could be if he truly stopped caring and suppressed the last vestiges of his conscience. The alternative view that actions still matter is explored (with variations) through all of the other characters who know about the resets. Most obviously by Maya Prime, who despite being an inherently selfish person who has watched countless versions of her friends come and go still can't help but see them as people.
View attachment 4273529
...
View attachment 4273530 View attachment 4273531 View attachment 4273532 View attachment 4273533
You could argue that this is a weakness of Maya's and that Nodoka has the strength to put emotions aside and approach the world from a detached and purely logical viewpoint. My reading is the opposite: Maya has shown strength in being able to maintain her humanity in a meaningless world. A central theme of LiL is that the notion of "real" and "unreal" is a false dichotomy and that true reality is determined by how people perceive things. If the world is real in the minds of its residents, then it's just as real as the world outside the simulation. If Nodoka's actions are real to those forced to experience them, then they matter just as much as if they had lasting consequences. After all, this is a game about Lessons in Love, not Lessons in Logic.

spoilers.title: Nodoka as a character
spoilers.html:
Okay, that's enough rambling about Nodoka as a person. I actually think all of the stuff that I've talked about are strengths of Nodoka as a character. Any good story needs bad people, and I enjoy how she's bad in different ways than Sensei and that's used to explore the game's themes. I also do like how she has been humanized a bit in recent updates, I just think we need to be careful not to let that overshadow everything that we've learned about her previously.

To finish things off, I do want to complain about the stuff that I still truly dislike about Nodoka's characterization: her genius and her "research".

Maybe it's just me, but I still find it impossible to be impressed by Nodoka's ability to "figure things out". We're never actual shown her process for learning anything (with one partial exception I'll talk about below), she just goes from not knowing things to knowing things whenever it's convenient for the story, and we still haven't been presented with any logical mechanism for how this happens. Here's what we've learned about her research:
  1. She forces people to confront new situations, the weirder the better, in order to observe how they react and to "confuse time" whatever that's supposed to actually accomplish.
  2. She's able to build up her research across resets through a combination of hidden journals and an ability to receive thoughts and/or memories directly from her past selves during her manic episodes.
The second point explains how she's able to retain knowledge, not how she gets it in the first place. The first point could explain how she seems to know everything about the game's characters and can predict how they'll react to her manipulation. (Though recently she's sucked at that, given the book plot with Futaba and the reveal with Io. There's also the issue that past Nodokas might have never met most of these people since according to Maya Prime she never joined the class before, but there's several possible explanations that get around that.) What it doesn't explain is how she could have learned anything about the world or anything supernatural.

It's fine for Nodoka's knowledge to be left mysterious. This is a game full of secrets and slow reveals. What I find infuriating is the story's insinuation that we should regard Nodoka as a super-genius who is so much better than everyone else because she solved mysteries using clues that no one else possessed, especially the reader.

One example to prove my point: we can almost see how a genius would have figured out Akira's relationship with Sekai. She heard Ami's poems on the beach and recognized their similarities to the Girl Who Cannot Breathe, which clued her in that TGWCB was Ami's mother. By reading TGWCB's poems and comparing them to what she knows about Akira's trauma, she figures out that he was "Boy" and was sexually abused. But where this falls apart is that she can't possibly have figured out from these anonymous poems that Sekai called him "Aki-kun", much less that this is a trigger for slipping. She also can't know this from trial and error in previous resets because both Akira's real name and the Akira+Sekai relationship were completely new to her when she learned them in this cycle.

Where could she have learned this? I see a few possibilities:
  • Divine revelation, most likely from Sekai herself.
  • Her mom's writings somehow talk about Akira and Sekai, maybe in Terminal 22. I think it's unlikely her mom would have known this much about their relationship, though.
  • She has access to another source of information that is completely hidden from the reader. I have a suspicion that her mom had some unpublished writings by Sekai (journals?) in her collection.
In any of these three cases, though, the information comes from an external source. Maybe she had to connect some dots, but as far as the reader knows she could have been straight up told everything.

So there's one thing that Nodoka might as well only know through divine revelation from the reader's perspective, and it's far from the only one. As long as she's allowed by the story to "just know things" why should we give her any credit for it?

I just played through the fiery scion recently and it was an adorable journey, really lighthearted fun. Also the writing has so many funny quirks, like him distributing jewelry like candy lol
In terms of writing, I'd recommend CosyCafe, the writing on that one makes little sense but it works if you take it as a lighthearted wholesome comedy. I also played Mist (completed), Now and Then (completed), To be a king, Khan and Radiant recently, and their stories held up more or less. AlwaysFan (completed) and Long Live the Princess (completed) are great ones in the regard of story too.

The most recent one I've finished is Wartribe Academy and I'm honestly on the fence with that one. The story is very engaging, but it is so engaging that I have deep issues with how it will resolve itself, as the potential for spetacular failure is high. You end up distrusting every single character and I'm afraid the author won't be able to follow up on all these betrayals in a satisfactory manner.

If you want the worst story possible though, as a sort of "now everything will seem good by comparison", I'd recommend either My New Family (sort of completed, but open ending) or DarkMagic. They're really atrocious.

Oh, I forgot to mention Ataegina (completed), it has branching paths and it is sort of like TFS, but less wholesome. It is currently undergoing a rework to enhance the endings so you might wait for that, but the endings are there regardless. Finally, I'm playing Crimson High at the moment, but I'm still in the beginning.

As a minor note, I played Corrupted Love, and if someone ever wondered how the dark route might go with the wizards that's pretty much the answer to it. Let's just say those 18 year olds don't really look like 18.
Also, I'd like to take the moment to advertise that I too will be replaying LiL during December. I'll make a post about it soon, but the general idea is to divide the four chapters between the 4/5 weeks of the month and discuss my findings through posts about it each week. So if anyone was waiting for an incentive to replay as well, this might be it, as I'll be discussing my findings all throughout December.
