To add to the many regulars that have already answered, LiL is not in fact an ero game. I mean, it is by definition, but not by focus.

LiL is a story about pedophilia and grooming, where supernatural aspects are introduced as a metaphor for trauma, compulsion and mental diseases. Following that, the harem (Akira Arakawa's many companions) also deals with many forms of trauma and abuse. All of these expand into what we can call lessons in love, not in a porn way, as one might expect, but in a form of heavy criticism and portrayal of the complications of many traumas intertwining in a sort of repeating purgatory that doubles as an extreme therapy session without a therapist.

That is a good description of the game imo: "throw a bunch of traumatized people into an neverending therapy session, that will reset them if they go to far/fail, until they can work through it all without a therapist's help, but only by having eachother".

(Although the supernatural angle should also be accounted for, the following turned into kind of a rant, so, if you want to skip it, the tldr is that the supernatural subplot to LiL has its place, but it's likely to be derivative/needlessly inflated).
Then there is the subplot of actual supernatural/occult/scientific things - this could end up being yet another manifestation of trauma, but in the case it isn't, it's never been the main focus either, as its elements are way too derivative to hold up as a main draw of the game. "There are two gods, but now there's a rope, but now there are three, but now there's an old one, but now there's shadow maya, but now there are many gods, but now there's a doppelganger, but now there is the world itself, but now there's a ghost, but now there's a a tree, but now there are things that shouldn't exist, but now there are things that can't be seen, but now there are things that can't be heard, but now there's..." - I could go on literally for an entire day. I'm not saying that the supernatural part should be ignored, but if one would define LiL by it, it would be akin to being interested in it mainly for the ramblings of a madman.

The main point of the supernatural, imo, is that is allows the setting of the repeating purgatory/infinite therapy session to exist. Everything else is basically decoration, don't get me wrong, it is entertaining decoration, good to discuss among ourselves and pass the time, a good mystery to solve together - but yeah, it's not why I play LiL.

Contrast it with Ghost in the Shell, Psycho-Pass, Neon Genesis Evangelion, hell, even Serial Experiments Lain, although I don't really like that one, or if we go into the actual books, Neuromancer - all those stories have a main focus that is aided by its secondary elements, there aren't many random elements thrown around just because. I fear LiL has A LOT of those, but we'll have to wait until the ending to form a proper opinion of course. Although, I think many will agree that when Selebus copies almost word for word scenes from Twin Peaks and other such movies/series, yeah, evidence kind of piles up on a lot of it being just "what am I going to throw around this month that kind of fits, but didn't really have to be here".

The main point of the supernatural, imo, is that is allows the setting of the repeating purgatory/infinite therapy session to exist. Everything else is basically decoration, don't get me wrong, it is entertaining decoration, good to discuss among ourselves and pass the time, a good mystery to solve together - but yeah, it's not why I play LiL.
Contrast it with
Ghost in the Shell
,
Psycho-Pass
,
Neon Genesis Evangelion
, hell, even
Serial Experiments Lain
, although I don't really like that one, or if we go into the actual books,
Neuromancer
- all those stories have a main focus that is aided by its secondary elements, there aren't many random elements thrown around just because. I fear LiL has
A LOT
of those, but we'll have to wait until the ending to form a proper opinion of course. Although, I think many will agree that when Selebus copies almost word for word scenes from
Twin Peaks
and other such movies/series, yeah, evidence kind of piles up on a lot of it being just "what am I going to throw around this month that kind of fits, but didn't really have to be here".

I had a much longer breakdown of individual trauma's for each character, but Moonflare's post went up when i was nearly done and covered most of the bases. So now I'm just expanding on the ones that needed more of a breakdown.

The Tsukioka's trauma is generational. Touka's the eldest daughter of a wealthy Japanese man with no sons. This means that she does not get to make her own choices. Her role is to be perfect and desirable so that she can be married off to an executive's son, who will then be adopted by the Tsukioka's and inherit the business. Her husband will be the Tsukioka heir, not her. Her job will be the Foundation. She already knows that her future husband (who will be chosen for her by her father, as it's a business decision) will be making decisions on her behalf.

Tsukasa laments being the "spare," if something happens to Touka, Touka's burden falls to Tsukasa. If Touka marries, Tsukasa is free to pursue her own goals, but right now she's in limbo. Touka, however, will never be free of that obligation. She will never be free to walk her own path.

Tsubasa grew up in the same situation, and knows the harm it did to her, and this is why she's trying to give Touka some room to breathe and make fun mistakes, because she's come out the other end of it and her life has very little joy in it because of that pressure.

Now, moving on to Otoha -- her parents are hyper-controlling. She's afraid to be herself around them. They've given her no room to breathe and grow. From experience -- this does a lot of long-term damage. A lot of people wind up in therapy as adults because their parents were like this. So it is a form of trauma, but it's not really conveyed well in-game.

When you start digging around in the "revenge rape" rabbit hole, shit gets dark super fast. She was essentially used as an example to other women "do as we say, or this happens to you."

posts.content_html_raw:
Moonflare said:
To add to the many regulars that have already answered, LiL is not in fact an ero game. I mean, it is by definition, but not by focus.

LiL is a story about pedophilia and grooming, where supernatural aspects are introduced as a metaphor for trauma, compulsion and mental diseases. Following that, the harem (Akira Arakawa's many companions) also deals with many forms of trauma and abuse. All of these expand into what we can call lessons in love, not in a porn way, as one might expect, but in a form of heavy criticism and portrayal of the complications of many traumas intertwining in a sort of repeating purgatory that doubles as an extreme therapy session without a therapist.

That is a good description of the game imo: "throw a bunch of traumatized people into an neverending therapy session, that will reset them if they go to far/fail, until they can work through it all without a therapist's help, but only by having eachother".

(Although the supernatural angle should also be accounted for, the following turned into kind of a rant, so, if you want to skip it, the tldr is that the supernatural subplot to LiL has its place, but it's likely to be derivative/needlessly inflated).
Then there is the subplot of actual supernatural/occult/scientific things - this could end up being yet another manifestation of trauma, but in the case it isn't, it's never been the main focus either, as its elements are way too derivative to hold up as a main draw of the game. "There are two gods, but now there's a rope, but now there are three, but now there's an old one, but now there's shadow maya, but now there are many gods, but now there's a doppelganger, but now there is the world itself, but now there's a ghost, but now there's a a tree, but now there are things that shouldn't exist, but now there are things that can't be seen, but now there are things that can't be heard, but now there's..." - I could go on literally for an entire day. I'm not saying that the supernatural part should be ignored, but if one would define LiL by it, it would be akin to being interested in it mainly for the ramblings of a madman.

The main point of the supernatural, imo, is that is allows the setting of the repeating purgatory/infinite therapy session to exist. Everything else is basically decoration, don't get me wrong, it is entertaining decoration, good to discuss among ourselves and pass the time, a good mystery to solve together - but yeah, it's not why I play LiL.

Contrast it with Ghost in the Shell, Psycho-Pass, Neon Genesis Evangelion, hell, even Serial Experiments Lain, although I don't really like that one, or if we go into the actual books, Neuromancer - all those stories have a main focus that is aided by its secondary elements, there aren't many random elements thrown around just because. I fear LiL has A LOT of those, but we'll have to wait until the ending to form a proper opinion of course. Although, I think many will agree that when Selebus copies almost word for word scenes from Twin Peaks and other such movies/series, yeah, evidence kind of piles up on a lot of it being just "what am I going to throw around this month that kind of fits, but didn't really have to be here".
Click to expand...
I would also say that LiL is not a traditional eroge while sexual aspect is a part that can't be removed since it's tethered unyieldingly with center of all things—Trauma and regret. I would use a simpler description for the game :"It's an endless and futile hope and dream of a group of people doomed from start for searching for happiness".

Supernatural subplot imo is clearly self-ironic, which servers both as an artifical gimmick (arbitary, sardonic and complicated revealing of hidden plot) and artistical manifestion of "truer" feelings. Therefore to me Happy Events in early days is an unique experience that couldn't be replicated by recent ones. God I miss the feeling I got when I read The Room with Clocks for the first time.

I think the most ambitious (and pretentious) attraction of LiL is that it tries to include everything, so much that text starts to form intertextuality with former itself — Everything is connected. With so many divergence, the story still tries to uphold a pure simultaneity — or, what amounts to the same thing, in an environment outside time altogether (cycling of time) — revealing the true meaning of “that which was, and which is and which shall be”.

I must stop ranting or everyone else would say I'm reading too much into (at the end of the day) a eroge, often forgot I started playing LiL only as another H-game, and in no time it turned to something I can't put my finger on

To add to the many regulars that have already answered, LiL is not in fact an ero game. I mean, it is by definition, but not by focus.

LiL is a story about pedophilia and grooming, where supernatural aspects are introduced as a metaphor for trauma, compulsion and mental diseases. That is a good description of the game imo: "throw a bunch of traumatized people into an neverending therapy session, that will reset them if they go to far/fail, until they can work through it all without a therapist's help, but only by having eachother".

(Although the supernatural angle should also be accounted for, the following turned into kind of a rant, so, if you want to skip it, the tldr is that the supernatural subplot to LiL has its place, but it's likely to be derivative/needlessly inflated).

"There are two gods, but now there's a rope, but now there are three, but now there's an old one, but now there's shadow maya, but now there are many gods, but now there's a doppelganger, but now there is the world itself, but now there's a ghost, but now there's a a tree, but now there are things that shouldn't exist, but now there are things that can't be seen, but now there are things that can't be heard, but now there's..." - I could go on literally for an entire day. I'm not saying that the supernatural part should be ignored, but if one would define LiL by it, it would be akin to being interested in it mainly for the ramblings of a madman.

Everything else is basically decoration, don't get me wrong, it is entertaining decoration, good to discuss among ourselves and pass the time, a good mystery to solve together - but yeah, it's not why I play LiL.

Contrast it with Ghost in the Shell, Psycho-Pass, Neon Genesis Evangelion, hell, even Serial Experiments Lain, although I don't really like that one, or if we go into the actual books, Neuromancer - all those stories have a main focus that is aided by its secondary elements, there aren't many random elements thrown around just because. I haven't seen your post on Niki, unless you're talking about the one where you ask people's playtimes. In that case, I thought it was just an observation which most of us agree with, Himawari did indeed imply that Niki wasn't real. Then again, Ami implies that no one is real but her and Akira. That being said, let's theorize a bit:
Okay so, here's what we know to be true: Maya shouldn't exist and hasn't existed from the start of the cycles, she was something that appeared/was conjured after some time. The fact that Maya existed before the cycles is either a memory corruption, or that after Maya first showed up, some sort of time travel happened in which she was conjured back into a world where Sekai died instead of marrying Akira.

Either way, this influences some characters, especially Noriko. In the world that Akira married Sekai, he wouldn't have been Noriko's tutor, as he'd have married Sekai before even becoming Niki's boyfriend. Our current Noriko has developed feeling for an Akira that only was her Akira because Maya was there. Aditionally, Niki also has only developed her dependency on Akira because he was affected by Sekai's death which held her back from actively pursuing him when he went off, and because of Maya that held him back from going back to her (by providing him with an outlet).

So, really, everyone we see in the current timeline could not only be considered sort of fake because of the nature of the simulation, but also because they're the versions of themselves from a corrupted reality (where Maya exists). The exception from all of this is Ami, as the main girl of the previous reality she remembers (at times at least) that all of this is fake. Kaori may be a second in line since she can grasp things beyond this reality due to being host to gods and it's even more telling that she can't even see Maya = she's unaffected by the Maya "corruption" of this timeline.

As I mentioned, I'm starting my third replay of LiL. This will be split throughout December until the next update rolls in:
Red: Chapter 1
Blue: Chapter 2
Green: Chapter 3
Pink: Chapter 4
White: Wiggle room
Yellow: Next update

For people that want to follow along, you should reach "Changing of Seasons" by Dec 8.
Then, you should reach "Utinam ne Illum" by Dec 15.

Next, you should reach "Remember to Smile" by Dec 22.
Finally, you should reach "What we'll see when we get there" by Dec 29.
Initially I had the idea to set a number of events per day, but given that real life is a thing, setting one chapter per week seems more doable. Also, chapter 4 has less events so it tracks that it falls on christmas week since we're all likely to have other activities then.

Each of the aforementioned weeks will then be flooded by me with posts about their respective chapters, as well as whoever wants to come along. This could just be a screenshot of something we find cute, had forgotten about, or more complex posts. My only recommendation is that you include the name of the event at some point in the post so that we can check it out as well (also because people that aren't replaying might be confused if you don't).

And that's all for now, get ready for a lot of flashback posts in the following month! (also, for the love of god, install/update the guide mod if you haven't).

posts.content_html_raw:
Moonflare said:
Do you think it's more likely that the first narrator is either Pareidolia or someone at the bottom of the well than that it's the Himawari that's within the cycles? Because there would be a Himawari outside of the cycles, and one that is at the waiting room (she shows up in the recent update, and it's where she's at in a flash during Ad Meliora). That would fit with the drain, and being unable to leave.

There is also the narrator from "Where the trees live", since "they" are the ones that send nao-chan, and they say they're speaking to him as people that are living in the same timeline as him, not from the future. It's either we have two Himawaris that narrate (one from the future and one from within the cycles), or the first narrator is narrating from the abyss? Which would make them either Pareidolia, Sekai or some version of Maya.
Click to expand...
I think (but can't know for sure) there's only one Himawari and she exists outside of the cycles. Time between different worlds doesn't run in parallel (this was shown conclusively when Sensei went to Terminal 22 before his own birth) so she's able to access our world at different points in the cycles while time moves normally in her world (not at the same rate). Given where and when she shows up, I think her ability to do things in this world is pretty limited.

I imagine the first narrator was in the well or an abyss of some sort before the start of the game but since then has been experiencing the world through Sensei. Maybe they ended up there after death - Ghost Sekai has said her afterlife is just an unending pool of darkness. It's unlikely it's any version of Sekai, though, since the narrator says they never liked poetry.

I'm unsure on the narrator's identity. I think there are a lot of little clues that point to Maya, but it's unlikely to be that simple based on the way the narrator speaks some of the time. Maya Prime would never in a million years (heh) talk like this:

...

...

Taken in isolation this passage really does sound like Himawari, but other things the narrator says don't sound like her to me. I find it hard to match their overall tone to any character.
The one thing I'm reasonably confident on (for reasons that are too complicated to try to write up right now) is that the narrator is connected to USER4, which probably makes them part of the "we" who sent Nao-chan. I personally don't think Himawari is part of this group, but I could be wrong. Leading candidates: Ami, Maya, a combined Ami and Maya, or someone we haven't met at all outside of narration.

In regards to the "Where the Trees Live" narrator: they say something like "I say this not as someone who knows the future but as someone experiencing the present with you". That doesn't mean that they exist in the cycles outside of watching through Sensei's eyes. It also doesn't necessarily mean that they don't know the/a future, just that it isn't influencing what they're currently saying.
Moonflare said:
Then we have the realities where Sekai is dead. Well, the difference between all of them is that when Sekai is alive, Maya doesn't exist. And when Sekai is dead, Maya is there. If we couple that with the fact that Ami seemed to have "Maya's place" in the cycles where Maya wasn't there, and the fact that Ami seemed to have been experiencing the cycles for much longer than Maya (the scary room scene in the last update), we can conclude that the cycles started from a reality where Maya didn't exist and Sekai was alive. Then, at some point, Maya started existing and the past got altered. I don't know if the past actually got altered, or it's just their memories of the past that did though.
Click to expand...
Technically we don't know for sure that Maya doesn't exist in the alternate timeline. It could be as simple as Sensei never had a relationship with her because Sekai was still around, which also means she never would have met Ami.

If Maya doesn't exist (probably the case), I think there's a simpler explanation for it: Sekai's death was the catalyst that led to Maya's creation, not the other way around. Because Sekai never died in this timeline, the events that led to Maya's existence never happened.

For one, if Sekai's dead there's a clear motive for Maya's creation, namely filling the hole in a broken Akira's life. I think it goes even further than that: before Maya's existence Akira filled the hole by having a sexual relationship with Ami. Eventually he was overcome by guilt and somehow changed the past to create Maya as the perfect wizard girlfriend so that at least the girl he abused wouldn't be the daughter he was supposed to protect.

I think that explains narrator Ami's reaction in "Wake Up (My Story)"; she's not saying that LiL as a whole is supposed to be her story, but rather this memory in particular. She's angry that Maya has replaced her in a scene which is supposed to show a relationship between wizard Ami and Akira. A scene that likely wouldn't have ever happened if Sekai was alive. It also explains why Ami doesn't appear in any of Akira's recovered memories; her original role has been "stolen" by Maya.

If you're correct that the alternate timeline shows the original main timeline before the past was altered, the change can't be as simple as Maya going back in time to cause Sekai's death. The divergence occurred long before that when Akira agreed/refused to go to Kyoto (or maybe even earlier). From what we saw, the most important thing that led to his decision not to go was his relationship with Niki. I don't see how a time traveling Maya could have affected it.

Instead I think this literally is an alternate timeline - a "what if" of Akira choosing to go to Kyoto. That's supported by the narrator talking about infinite worlds that exist as a "library of outcomes" where things happened slightly differently.
Moonflare said:
She keeps rebooting because she's also a shadow, according to Ami, at least. It was implied that the main characters of the cycles were Akira and Ami. Sekai, as everyone else, only had a part to play. If you remember correctly, Sekai mentioned the police and Ami ruining everything for them - her concerns are regarding real world consequences, whereas Ami is aware that everything is playing in repeat.
Click to expand...
I interpret these lines to mean that alternate timeline Sekai knows that the world has to be reset as a result of Ami's actions.
Ami was looking forward to Christmas but now it's not going to happen "this year" because time is about to be rolled back to earlier in 2020 by "SANTA", which I assume means god(s).

posts.content_html_raw:
third replay has started, this post deals with an old goth chick crying at some words, and the identity of the first narrator of the game, and why her name is Ami/Amy the second.

In the past I have talked about how it was only during my second playthrough that I started to love LiL, but that is incorrect at least regarding my first impression of it. Sure, there was a lot that I scoffed at during my first time (like Yasu and the gods' nonsense), a lot I skipped entirely (like Chika's storyline), but this, this had me from the start:
I remember reading every sentence out loud, because the music captivated me so much that I decided to really give my all this time. Rarely would I would this with a porn game, hell, it's even rare for me to do it with a proper novel. But here I was reading word for word out loud, with no idea what would come next and we have first the idea of perception, how the correct angle of light can make invisible things visible; then we have the romantization of death (which spawned so many theories that Akira jumped to his death at the beginning of the game), but here's where all the hairs of my arm never fail to stand up: "the third thing I can never understand is you".

Man, what a strong start to a narrative. I wonder how many times Selebus rewrote this. It's just so powerful! "because where you're going is somewhere special. Somewhere with so much strangeness in every single one of its proportions that you'll be forced to understand how truly beautiful life can be, even during its darkest moments." It's haunting.

Then as we get to the "I'm supposed to tell you that nothing is real. We're all just air. So, how about we breathe together?" I start crying like a child. This is one seriously amazing start.

On another note though, yet again, upon seeing the entire event I'm convinced this is Himawari, here is my evidence:
this is sort of what she talks about during "Ad Meliora".


then we have her addressing poetry, and Himawari also tells us she can't do poetry during chapter 3, in the event where she ends by telling us her eyes are blue.


Himawari loves Akira, and yet is the one character that is not romantically in love with him, despite still loving him. Also they barely know eachother because he either hasn't met her, or she spent little time with him, being raised by her mom.


It's Himawari's job (as told in the event in the beach, where she talks about Shiori), and the way to address herself as a mysterious narrator echoes what she says to Ayane about being a mysterious guide. Not knowing if they'll meet for real also falls in line with her not being a god, or a being with higher power. She'd like to, but it's not up to her.


Okay, this is a lot to unpack, so let's take it step by step.

Himawari has a history of being forced to do stuff, and also of finding loopholes to teach Akira stuff during these duties. The most famous one is after the church quiz, in which she teaches us that his mind doesn't get broken by memories, but by how he feels about them, before putting a flower in his pocket to help him.

Now, what she's doing here is that she's OBLIGATED to tell him that nothing is real. She always says she's being forced to do something when that is the case, from which we can tell that this isn't actual the case that nothing is real, because look at what she says after it: "we're all just air, so how about we breathe together?".

This is directly opposed to the idea that nothing is real, she's telling him to behave as if everything is real/has importance. It's not that he's the single person in a playground, but that they're all the same.


Remember that Himawari's place in Akira's life is "everything you never wanted, but all that you'll ever need" (granted this refers to the idea of him having any child, so it could be applied to Ami, but it fits here). And I bring this up because you tell me if this isn't prime daughter behavior:


Here we have motivation if you choose to say you're not ready, and other people just don't fit here imo. Neither Ami nor Maya would talk like this I think. Also because they're already out since no romantic love, but the point stands. They're closer than he thinks, and they believe in him completely. Daughter behavior.


This is sort of what Himawari tells him to do when they meet at the beach as well:


One thing though that we tend to forget is that this narrator is talking by Akira's side on the rooftop from where he jumps. Himawari has been seen on the rooftop when she intercepts Nodoka, so it's not like she hasn't ever been there. Every supernatural thing seems to take place at the school, including the room with the clocks, with Himawari waiting at the exit. And we could interpret that the narration takes place with them going up the stairs to the rooftop, until Akira opens his eyes to see the sky outside.

tldr of who the narrator is:

Moonflare said:
this is sort of what she talks about during "Ad Meliora".
View attachment 4298960
Click to expand...
I'm not sure what you mean here. During "Ad Meliora" she says she's lonely, but that's part of her attempt to seduce Sensei while pretending to be Sana, she's definitely not speaking for herself. Maybe I missed something.
Moonflare said:
then we have her addressing poetry, and Himawari also tells us she can't do poetry during chapter 3, in the event where she ends by telling us her eyes are blue.
View attachment 4298966
Click to expand...
There's a big difference between disliking poetry and being bad at writing it. If anything, I'd think the fact that she admires her dad's poetry and makes an attempt at a poem indicates that she does have some interest in it.
Moonflare said:
Himawari loves Akira, and yet is the one character that is not romantically in love with him, despite still loving him. Also they barely know eachother because he either hasn't met her, or she spent little time with him, being raised by her mom.
View attachment 4298968
Click to expand...
The romantic love thing is probably the strongest argument for Himawari, but I can't see how she would say "we barely even know each other" when she has numerous fond memories of her father (see e.g. her narration in "Parallelogram" and "Irregular Heartbeat"). The "I love that you're here" bit also kind of implies that this is a new love born from the situation, rather than preexisting familial love, but I could be reading too much into that.
Moonflare said:
It's Himawari's job (as told in the event in the beach, where she talks about Shiori), and the way to address herself as a mysterious narrator echoes what she says to Ayane about being a mysterious guide. Not knowing if they'll meet for real also falls in line with her not being a god, or a being with higher power. She'd like to, but it's not up to her.
View attachment 4298970
Click to expand...
As far as I can tell, her job is to be Pareidolia's errand girl - a job she probably took so that she could have access to the world and help while bending/breaking the rules. It's possible she's not even supposed to be a narrator, if she's who Long Maya was talking about in Sensei Quest, with "coloring outside the lines" referring to how she breaks rules. Though it would be hilarious if Long Maya is talking about Nao-chan and saying that she's shit at drawing.
Moonflare said:
Himawari has a history of being forced to do stuff, and also of finding loopholes to teach Akira stuff during these duties. The most famous one is after the church quiz, in which she teaches us that his mind doesn't get broken by memories, but by how he feels about them, before putting a flower in his pocket to help him.
Click to expand...
I'm actually 50/50 on whether the "World of Lines" narrator is Himawari or not. "I have felt comfort in you even when you thought I never would" sounds more like Ami than Himawari with her apparently happy family dynamic (see "Irregular Heartbeat"), and remember that the other photo in Akira's pocket is Ami in a field of sunflowers. Anyway, I agree with your point about breaking the rules, so this isn't very important right now. I do think other narrators have also talked about needing to follow rules, but I can't point to any specific event off the top of my head.
Moonflare said:
Now, what she's doing here is that she's OBLIGATED to tell him that nothing is real. She always says she's being forced to do something when that is the case, from which we can tell that this isn't actual the case that nothing is real, because look at what she says after it: "we're all just air, so how about we breathe together?".

This is directly opposed to the idea that nothing is real, she's telling him to behave as if everything is real/has importance. It's not that he's the single person in a playground, but that they're all the same.
View attachment 4298980
Click to expand...
I think this passage points to Maya a lot more than it does Himawari. On a few occassions, Maya has told Sensei that nothing is real even though she clearly doesn't believe it.

...

...

...
I think she does this because Senseis who treat things seriously and act as responsible teachers don't survive; she needs him to "fail" morally in order to stick around.

...
Also note that at the point Maya when says "you've been told time and time again" that nothing is real, she's only actually said that to him once before. She knows what the narrator has been telling him unless we're supposed to assume that this is something that she keeps saying off screen.

Breathing together also somewhat points to Maya. Sensei thinks about it while he's on the roof with her, though it's unclear whether he's thinking about Maya, Sekai, or someone else entirely.
Moonflare said:
Remember that Himawari's place in Akira's life is "everything you never wanted, but all that you'll ever need" (granted this refers to the idea of him having any child, so it could be applied to Ami, but it fits here).
Click to expand...
Another digression: that line is from the narration in "Cicadian Rhythm", which I find confusing to say the least. The tone doesn't sound at all like Himawari to me; the narrator says they broke a rule "tonight" but it was the previous night that Himawari saved Ayane; the narrator calls themselves moonlight and the shadow following Akira, both of which are symbols used for Sekai; the narrator says they don't exist and are only in Akira's head whereas Himawari lives with her mother.

On the other hand, this is from the same beach trip where Himawari narrates "Hyzenthlay" and "Flowerchild" and she's a big fan of breaking rules. But would she really call herself "all that you'll ever need" when she definitely thinks that he needs Ayane?
Moonflare said:
And I bring this up because you tell me if this isn't prime daughter behavior:
View attachment 4298982
Click to expand...
This is a good argument for Himawari, who also says that she hopes he's having fun in "Irregular Heartbeat".
Moonflare said:
Here we have motivation if you choose to say you're not ready, and other people just don't fit here imo. Neither Ami nor Maya would talk like this I think. Also because they're already out since no romantic love, but the point stands. They're closer than he thinks, and they believe in him completely. Daughter behavior.
View attachment 4298985
Click to expand...
A lack of romantic love probably rules out Ami Prime and Maya Prime but not necessarily their version(s) from outside the simulation. "Closer than you think" does make sense as a family member, I agree with that. Random thought: Yuu is a family member who could realistically say that he and Akira barely know each other. This just occurred to me so I haven't thought through whether he works with other clues.
Moonflare said:
One thing though that we tend to forget is that this narrator is talking by Akira's side on the rooftop from where he jumps.
Click to expand...
I don't think there's any evidence that the narrator is physically there rather than in his head. Just like the other narrators, Himawari typically (always?) narrates while she's not in the same place as Akira.
Moonflare said:
Every supernatural thing seems to take place at the school, including the room with the clocks, with Himawari waiting at the exit.
Click to expand...
What's the evidence that the room with clocks is at the school? I think it's far more likely that it's in the wishing well; remember that the room is "at the bottom of everything" and in one the scenes there the upside down house is visible right-side up through the window. In any case, happy events which have an identifiable location often occur at the abandoned school, which is a completely different place from Sensei's school and has also been described as "the bottom of everything".

You know, my first impulse was to give you a snarky no.

But hey, reasonable question, so....

It's a very well-written looooong metaphysical (or maybe psychological) horror VN with themes of pedophilia and hebephilia, where the MC is both an abuse victim and an abuser, and is struggling with that (among many other things). Oh, and there's some sex with questionably of-age girls (at least one of whom he's directly related to), and even a grown woman or three.

But this is definitely not a game for getting your jollies quickly.

I noticed the same situations with Ami but I interpreted them differently. To me, they were rather showing how oblivious the early game Ami is and how she reacts relatively naturally to Akira's situation (given her general character). I don't feel like she is manipulating him into any direction at all.
Some sentences and wordings do seem like foreshadowing, but in my opinion they were deliberately placed by Sel (I mentioned some of them in one of my earlier Replay posts) and not something Ami was supposed to be consciously aware of.

I'm no expert at psychology, but wouldn't you say a lot of these instances could fall under the concept of confirmation bias?
What I mean by that is that once you obtain future knowledge, looking back into the past, you jump to conclusion and interpret situations fitting a pattern that you already established in your head.
I'm not saying that all of your examples apply to that, it's possible that some of them might really be Ami being aware of resets and decides to hint at that fact. But why would she even do that? What's there to gain for her, other than risking Akira recalling prior memories and Maya becoming even more suspicious of her?
It doesn't really sit right with me and I personally registered them as either coincidences that I just forcefully connected with current theories and knowledge or simply as Sel being an egomaniac Sel who wants to prove to people who replay the game that he was so wise and mindful to hint at future events and developments early in the game.

Now in terms of Maya, definitely, she is hinting at that stuff constantly, almost teasing Akira with it in the hopes to awaken his memories and challenging him to become more than the boring niece-fucking husk of himself that she had to endure for the past GODgod-knows-how-many cycles.

Anyways, keep the posts coming!
I will try to continue my run hopefully today as well.

Moonflare said:
third replay has started, this post deals with an old goth chick crying at some words, and the identity of the first narrator of the game, and why her name is Ami/Amy the second.

In the past I have talked about how it was only during my second playthrough that I started to love LiL, but that is incorrect at least regarding my first impression of it. Sure, there was a lot that I scoffed at during my first time (like Yasu and the gods' nonsense), a lot I skipped entirely (like Chika's storyline), but this, this had me from the start:
View attachment 4298932
I remember reading every sentence out loud, because the music captivated me so much that I decided to really give my all this time. Rarely would I would this with a porn game, hell, it's even rare for me to do it with a proper novel. But here I was reading word for word out loud, with no idea what would come next and we have first the idea of perception, how the correct angle of light can make invisible things visible; then we have the romantization of death (which spawned so many theories that Akira jumped to his death at the beginning of the game), but here's where all the hairs of my arm never fail to stand up: "the third thing I can never understand is you".

Man, what a strong start to a narrative. I wonder how many times Selebus rewrote this. It's just so powerful! "because where you're going is somewhere special. Somewhere with so much strangeness in every single one of its proportions that you'll be forced to understand how truly beautiful life can be, even during its darkest moments." It's haunting.

Then as we get to the "I'm supposed to tell you that nothing is real. We're all just air. So, how about we breathe together?" I start crying like a child. This is one seriously amazing start.

On another note though, yet again, upon seeing the entire event I'm convinced this is Himawari, here is my evidence:
this is sort of what she talks about during "Ad Meliora".
View attachment 4298960

then we have her addressing poetry, and Himawari also tells us she can't do poetry during chapter 3, in the event where she ends by telling us her eyes are blue.
View attachment 4298966

Himawari loves Akira, and yet is the one character that is not romantically in love with him, despite still loving him. Also they barely know eachother because he either hasn't met her, or she spent little time with him, being raised by her mom.
View attachment 4298968

It's Himawari's job (as told in the event in the beach, where she talks about Shiori), and the way to address herself as a mysterious narrator echoes what she says to Ayane about being a mysterious guide. Not knowing if they'll meet for real also falls in line with her not being a god, or a being with higher power. She'd like to, but it's not up to her.
View attachment 4298970

Okay, this is a lot to unpack, so let's take it step by step.

Himawari has a history of being forced to do stuff, and also of finding loopholes to teach Akira stuff during these duties. The most famous one is after the church quiz, in which she teaches us that his mind doesn't get broken by memories, but by how he feels about them, before putting a flower in his pocket to help him.

Now, what she's doing here is that she's OBLIGATED to tell him that nothing is real. She always says she's being forced to do something when that is the case, from which we can tell that this isn't actual the case that nothing is real, because look at what she says after it: "we're all just air, so how about we breathe together?".

This is directly opposed to the idea that nothing is real, she's telling him to behave as if everything is real/has importance. It's not that he's the single person in a playground, but that they're all the same.
View attachment 4298980

Remember that Himawari's place in Akira's life is "everything you never wanted, but all that you'll ever need" (granted this refers to the idea of him having any child, so it could be applied to Ami, but it fits here). And I bring this up because you tell me if this isn't prime daughter behavior:
View attachment 4298982

Here we have motivation if you choose to say you're not ready, and other people just don't fit here imo. Neither Ami nor Maya would talk like this I think. Also because they're already out since no romantic love, but the point stands. They're closer than he thinks, and they believe in him completely. Daughter behavior.
View attachment 4298985

View attachment 4299002

Every supernatural thing seems to take place at the school, including the room with the clocks, with Himawari waiting at the exit. And we could interpret that the narration takes place with them going up the stairs to the rooftop, until Akira opens his eyes to see the sky outside.

posts.content_html_raw:
Many people commented on my findings about Ami and Himawari, I unfortunately will not be writing in-depth replies as I'm on a tight schedule just to play the game and report what I find (also because some of the regulars have already replied and provided explanations).
But simply put, on the confirmation bias (which was a common point), I'm giving Selebus the benefit of the doubt. We have all already operated on the assumption that Ami didn't know anything, and I am now operating on the assumption that she did. When I finally reach the current update, I'll be able to see whichever one holds up better. I think it's more likely that Selebus is retconning a lot of stuff, but as I said, I'm giving him the benefit of the doubt, and will only reform my opinion when I'm finished with the current replay.

The Himawari counter-arguments have all been provided by aramaug, I think the one thing he didn't touch on was about Himawari putting Akira through hell? Well, this has also been partially answered by the regulars already, but basically, this comes from two primary sources.

The first is that Himawari (mostly through narration) explains that Akira has to go through a lot of suffering so that she can create a better world (although she does try to make it less suffering whenever she can) - you can see this clearly on her dialogue with Long Maya, when Akira has to answer their quiz about the girls.

The second is that Himawari is involved herself in the manipulation of this cycle (most notably through the scarf), but also through a lot of other stuff. Like having a stand in "three halves make a whole", and influencing Nodoka. So, in that sense, she's the one putting our Akira through stuff, because she's engineering his trials, more or less (although how much of this is under orders we don't know).
Random notes on the replay that didn't merit their own posts:
1. Maya notes that Akira is guided on purpose to the shrine in his first outing out of the house. You literally cannot go anywhere else.

2. The upside down house's first mention happens in a dorm event with Chika "side event", in which they watch the house with five girls looking for something, one of them is crying, and there is something in the attic. Maya also says she's been dreaming of things being upside down.

3. The event in which Akira is called to step out into the static, and is saved by Yumi, is what awards him with a meeting with "redacted" in the "Room with the Clocks". Following this event, Yumi goes to talk to Maya during lunch, in which she calls her "Ponytail". In the room with the clocks, Sekai makes her first appearance and also calls Maya "the ponytail bitch".

4. Akira notices Niki's poster when visiting Chika, so much so that he is unable to hug Chika back but quickly forgets about it. When dating Makoto (after slipping in front of the porn shop), he goes to sleep thinking of someone else (although it isn't clear if he was thinking about Sekai or Niki - but there are Niki's posters throughout the city).

5. Akira is a very cool bro to Rin when he finds her having a sort of date with Chika in the café. He helps her along and leaves not wanting to interrupt.

6. Makoto is the one that asks Akira on a date first, but when Yumi sees them at the park, it wasn't by design. They just happened to stumble upon eachother. This event is what leads to "the town has two halves".

7. Other than Yumi being called to many detentions before the cycles, Akira also used to hang with Futaba on the weekends by the library. So far, it's only these two that seemed to be around him other than the usual suspects, which would be yet another reason for Yumi's distaste of Futaba (since she tends to attack and be particularly offended by the prospect of Akira being interested in her).

8. Until Yumi is assaulted by Akira, she seemed genuinely on the fence about him, despite her hostility. It is likely that if he hadn't assaulted her, she'd crumble very quickly. "The town has two halves" also seems to be the first major emulation of Sekai by Akira, so although Nodoka's compulsion explanation fits, it may be either one or both.

9. Kaori's first meeting with Ami has her being extra caring for her, and Ami can also feel a special kinship towards her. It was obviously impossible to tell it at the time, but Kaori tells Akira many times over things Sekai would about their little girl. Like taking care of her, and treating Ami from the start as his girlfriend.

10. Everyone knows I like Sara, but yeah. I like Sara. Her introduction as supermom is cute. And also it is a very early show of Sana's inner self, as she hides that Akira is a dude from her, and insists that they don't meet more often.

11. Akira's meeting with Miku on the weekend has him saying that he doesn't like soccer, which is probably the reason he has a harder time with Karin in this cycle. The conversation starts with Miku trying to pawn Karin off to him in exchange for him becoming their coach, which is possibly what happened in that one timeline where they're fucking, and it was likely due to Miku's plan being accepted. Since he doesn't like soccer here, he ends up fucking Kirin instead.

12. By my estimations, the first girl Akira kisses is always Ayane. Followed by possibly Chika on the event where she has to rush home to help Chinami. What is notable about that event is that if you choose to kiss her, the system asks when you're going to be able to find what's buried underneath your feet. And if you don't, it says you're a coward and you'll never be able to find it. Given that Sekai is what's buried, it would follow that it is by acting as a total degenerate that Akira would get in touch with these memories? I don't know. I also don't know what the flashes of Chika crying then are supposed to represent.

13. Also by my estimations, the first sexual contact between Akira and a student is with Makoto, by her giving him a handjob while masturbating at the secret room of the porn shop. But it's possible this could change depending on the event order, I'm not sure. I recall someone saying that Ami is always the first, but maybe that was about actual sex. I guess we'll see.

Bias and Himawari

Okay so, Ami definitely knew what was up, it's extremely obvious in the replay. There's this event called "something darker". I'll give a rundown.

Ami starts blasting Niki's song while on her underwear, she hears Akira knocking on the door, but ignores it so that he has to come in. Akira starts imagining Niki while listening to the song, and Ami keeps flirting with him until he stops imagining Niki to just focusing on Ami. This is all a calculated move, mind you, including the song.

Then, Akira asks her what family is, and he realises he fucked up because he just asked someone with only one person left what family was. Surprisingly, Ami calls him a pervert. This is yet another indication that this has happened before, as someone in her position wouldn't naturally go this way upon being asked that - she basically ignores it and doubles down on her seduction tactic. Ami goes on to say that she will just have to satisfy him as long as he doesn't involve himself with anyone else (which is the deal he takes on the Karin world).
During this conversation Akira notes that she's trying to entrap him and that she's way smarter than she pretends to be. Then he slips and finds himself on top of her. This slip is very likely to have been Nodoka's compulsion, he's repeating what he has done multiple times in previous cycles (attacking Ami, which Maya mentioned that she's always the first, and most of the time he barely leaves the house after falling for her, which means this plan works - also, important to note that Ami's likely always the first because she makes it so with this event everytime).
Then when Akira asks her why she's so sure he won't hurt her, she starts monologuing about how their minds/bodies won't even allow it to happen. Which, in retrospect/in context, she's clearly talking about previous Akiras that all fell for this ploy. That's when everything changes because Akira LEAVES.
This is genius because, it's so freaking obvious:
Ami isn't confused about Akira pushing her down, she's confused as to why he didn't follow through for the first time in countless cycles. All of this was a planned out routine that always works. Something is different with this Akira. He controlled himself and went away. This is what she's confused about.

I think one might even say that she is the something darker. Akira, after all, was able to resist the trap she set up for him, he's something "lighter" than the Akiras she's used to.

Many people commented on my findings about Ami and Himawari, I unfortunately will not be writing in-depth replies as I'm on a tight schedule just to play the game and report what I find (also because some of the regulars have already replied and provided explanations).
But simply put, on the confirmation bias (which was a common point), I'm giving Selebus the benefit of the doubt. We have all already operated on the assumption that Ami didn't know anything, and I am now operating on the assumption that she did. When I finally reach the current update, I'll be able to see whichever one holds up better. I think it's more likely that Selebus is retconning a lot of stuff, but as I said, I'm giving him the benefit of the doubt, and will only reform my opinion when I'm finished with the current replay.

The Himawari counter-arguments have all been provided by aramaug, I think the one thing he didn't touch on was about Himawari putting Akira through hell? Well, this has also been partially answered by the regulars already, but basically, this comes from two primary sources.

The first is that Himawari (mostly through narration) explains that Akira has to go through a lot of suffering so that she can create a better world (although she does try to make it less suffering whenever she can) - you can see this clearly on her dialogue with Long Maya, when Akira has to answer their quiz about the girls.

The second is that Himawari is involved herself in the manipulation of this cycle (most notably through the scarf), but also through a lot of other stuff. Like having a stand in "three halves make a whole", and influencing Nodoka. So, in that sense, she's the one putting our Akira through stuff, because she's engineering his trials, more or less (although how much of this is under orders we don't know).
Random notes on the replay that didn't merit their own posts:
1. Maya notes that Akira is guided on purpose to the shrine in his first outing out of the house. You literally cannot go anywhere else.

2. The upside down house's first mention happens in a dorm event with Chika "side event", in which they watch the house with five girls looking for something, one of them is crying, and there is something in the attic. Maya also says she's been dreaming of things being upside down.

3. The event in which Akira is called to step out into the static, and is saved by Yumi, is what awards him with a meeting with "redacted" in the "Room with the Clocks". Following this event, Yumi goes to talk to Maya during lunch, in which she calls her "Ponytail". In the room with the clocks, Sekai makes her first appearance and also calls Maya "the ponytail bitch".

4. Akira notices Niki's poster when visiting Chika, so much so that he is unable to hug Chika back but quickly forgets about it. When dating Makoto (after slipping in front of the porn shop), he goes to sleep thinking of someone else (although it isn't clear if he was thinking about Sekai or Niki - but there are Niki's posters throughout the city).

5. Akira is a very cool bro to Rin when he finds her having a sort of date with Chika in the café. He helps her along and leaves not wanting to interrupt.

6. Makoto is the one that asks Akira on a date first, but when Yumi sees them at the park, it wasn't by design. They just happened to stumble upon eachother. This event is what leads to "the town has two halves".

7. Other than Yumi being called to many detentions before the cycles, Akira also used to hang with Futaba on the weekends by the library. So far, it's only these two that seemed to be around him other than the usual suspects, which would be yet another reason for Yumi's distaste of Futaba (since she tends to attack and be particularly offended by the prospect of Akira being interested in her).

8. Until Yumi is assaulted by Akira, she seemed genuinely on the fence about him, despite her hostility. It is likely that if he hadn't assaulted her, she'd crumble very quickly. "The town has two halves" also seems to be the first major emulation of Sekai by Akira, so although Nodoka's compulsion explanation fits, it may be either one or both.

9. Kaori's first meeting with Ami has her being extra caring for her, and Ami can also feel a special kinship towards her. It was obviously impossible to tell it at the time, but Kaori tells Akira many times over things Sekai would about their little girl. Like taking care of her, and treating Ami from the start as his girlfriend.

10. Everyone knows I like Sara, but yeah. I like Sara. Her introduction as supermom is cute. And also it is a very early show of Sana's inner self, as she hides that Akira is a dude from her, and insists that they don't meet more often.

11. Akira's meeting with Miku on the weekend has him saying that he doesn't like soccer, which is probably the reason he has a harder time with Karin in this cycle. The conversation starts with Miku trying to pawn Karin off to him in exchange for him becoming their coach, which is possibly what happened in that one timeline where they're fucking, and it was likely due to Miku's plan being accepted. Since he doesn't like soccer here, he ends up fucking Kirin instead.

12. By my estimations, the first girl Akira kisses is always Ayane. Followed by possibly Chika on the event where she has to rush home to help Chinami. What is notable about that event is that if you choose to kiss her, the system asks when you're going to be able to find what's buried underneath your feet. And if you don't, it says you're a coward and you'll never be able to find it. Given that Sekai is what's buried, it would follow that it is by acting as a total degenerate that Akira would get in touch with these memories? I don't know. I also don't know what the flashes of Chika crying then are supposed to represent.

13. Also by my estimations, the first sexual contact between Akira and a student is with Makoto, by her giving him a handjob while masturbating at the secret room of the porn shop. But it's possible this could change depending on the event order, I'm not sure. I recall someone saying that Ami is always the first, but maybe that was about actual sex. I guess we'll see.

14. There is a lot of foreshadowing about Sekai's death during the beginning of the game, especially when Akira goes extra predator and starts musing about making decisions with a piece of glass from a broken windshield, or something. This has been used plenty of times already.

15. This is most likely nothing, but Ami compares Maya to an all consuming orb, or something like that. Which, well, we've seen an all consuming orb very recently. It would certainly explain Maya's need to eat everything all the time, but it's unlikely to mean anything.

I think that's the more notable stuff for now.

spoilers.title: Bias and Himawari
spoilers.html:
But simply put, on the confirmation bias (which was a common point), I'm giving Selebus the benefit of the doubt. We have all already operated on the assumption that Ami didn't know anything, and I am now operating on the assumption that she did. When I finally reach the current update, I'll be able to see whichever one holds up better. I think it's more likely that Selebus is retconning a lot of stuff, but as I said, I'm giving him the benefit of the doubt, and will only reform my opinion when I'm finished with the current replay.

The Himawari counter-arguments have all been provided by aramaug, I think the one thing he didn't touch on was about Himawari putting Akira through hell? Well, this has also been partially answered by the regulars already, but basically, this comes from two primary sources.

The first is that Himawari (mostly through narration) explains that Akira has to go through a lot of suffering so that she can create a better world (although she does try to make it less suffering whenever she can) - you can see this clearly on her dialogue with Long Maya, when Akira has to answer their quiz about the girls.

The second is that Himawari is involved herself in the manipulation of this cycle (most notably through the scarf), but also through a lot of other stuff. Like having a stand in "three halves make a whole", and influencing Nodoka. So, in that sense, she's the one putting our Akira through stuff, because she's engineering his trials, more or less (although how much of this is under orders we don't know).

Moonflare said:
Okay so, Ami definitely knew what was up, it's extremely obvious in the replay. There's this event called "something darker". I'll give a rundown.
Click to expand...
I was thinking the other day about "How would I make sense of Ami's situation without assuming her being all-knowing since the very beginning?". The struggle I always have is that, despite having a good amount of suspicious moments, there are still a considerably large amount of early Ami moments that don't sit well with that assumption; Ami being more crucial than she appears to be has always been an obvious theme, but “Ami knowing what was up ever since the beginning" is such a tough pill to swallow that I don't think I'd buy it without some heavy cherry picking (ex: arguments like "well she clearly knew shit in this event and she clearly was faking it in that event") or until some more defined evidences that support the same thing.

Then, I thought of Maya's interpretation of "Why girls already had preconceived notions of the type of person Sensei was", "Why girls quicky warmed up to a Sensei that underwent a complete switch in personalities", and "Why everyone just decided that not being taught anymore was ok" (all from her event Now More Than Ever). My understanding of her theory is that even if an iteration got hard reset and girls' memories were accordingly reformatted, their brains could still quickly adapt to a new iteration because, from a higher dimension perspective, most things the next iteration would do to/with the girls would not be their first time; they lost access to those specific memories but it doesn't mean they would feel unfamiliar once the next iteration starts repeating similar actions.

Originally, this event I think was supposed to be Maya implying why Sensei can advance with every girl so quickly without any hiccup, but potentially this can be applicable to Ami's situation. Via the same mechanism, Ami can quickly accept a new slate-cleaned iteration that knows literally nothing about anything, and quickly accept him starting to lust over her, without needing to know "how things were supposed to be one or a few apocalypses ago" or rather, "what apocalypses themselves are". This train of thoughts relies on at least two things: Maya's theory being correct and Maya holds the "correct" memories of what kind of a person "the original Sensei" was (aka, a correct frame of reference capable of attributing girl's quick adaptation to this memory reformatting theory instead of simply the kind of person Akira already was pre-resets). Her knowledge admittedly has not been impeccable, but in this case it's an easier sell for me to use her theory to rationalize early Ami moments in comparison to assuming the Ami since the beginning knows as much as the Ami that tortures New Maya.

skwada said:
If you could go back in time and stop yourself from ever playing LiL and magically guarantee that you would never learn of its existence, would you?

I think I would because the content you consume paints your mind, and spending hundreds of hours over the course of multiple years on LiL definitely paints your mind. I can't speak for others of course, but despite all the beautiful moments in LiL, Akira's depression, self-hatred, and constant negative self-talk surely has a net negative impact on my mental state as a reader. It varies heavily based on what is going on with my life at the time but I usually at least feel sad and worthless for a few hours after reading the dark scenes.

Honestly I've been thinking of quitting for some time now, and given what's probably gonna happen in the next update, it's as good a time as any. I think Sel will probably execute it in a way similar to Stomach Ache, in which case I think I'd be able to digest it just fine. But at the same time, sometimes playing this game makes me question what the fuck I'm doing with my life. At the current rate, I'll never achieve my ultimate life-goal of building a harem of catgirls...

Fuck!!
Click to expand...
The night is darkest before the dawn. Although I am not personally trapped by the natural human proclivity to start to believe a thesis can only exist with its antithesis (e.g. tripe like 'there can be no peace without war,' 'there can be no happiness without suffering,' etc) it is undeniable that this manner of synergetic thinking has immense power over our psyches, and so when they can be used as tools it is beneficial to do so. Selebus is (unfortunately) imprisoned with the demons of his mind and has no choice but to fight a noble battle to see beauty within the darkness, to make the silver lining of clouds shine brighter than any stormy sky, and so on, with Lessons in Love being allegorical to these struggles. It is my opinion that being exposed to this darkness and being taught to find the light (in this case 'love') is likely a rather valuable life tool. A thought-provoking line from early in LiL is the narrator interrupting a happy scene to mockingly ask, "Why does this scare you? It's a game. You should be more scared about a real loved one dying." (or something to that effect). Although it is easy to interpret this merely as a flippant breaking of the fourth wall, careful analysis reveals a surprising amount of depth. Why /do/ people get so affected by fiction when real life is horrible enough? Why /do/ we fear the deaths of fictional characters sometimes more than we do the deaths of those in real life? Why /does/ everyone know death is inevitable yet ignore it? The sad, painful reality is that everything horrible in LiL reflects horrible things in real life that could happen to you or anyone at any point (abstractly - not referring to the so-called time loop here.) In many cases it will be beneficial to be equipped to face these demons. The worthlessness you feel after scenes, and the process of regaining strength afterwards, may be strengthening some part of your spirit such that over time you will be Stronger. You will have Grown. And thanks to that, you may be able to Survive.

So it's probably a good idea to play Lessons in Love and I wouldn't stop myself or most people even if I could. That said, most of the above doesn't apply to me since I am blessed with a spotless mind free of any demons or torment. The warm blanket of alexithymia keeps me safe even during the darkest and coldest nights. For me, and perhaps many of the more flippant users of this forum, Lessons in Love serves as fine entertainment and literature above all else. Some of the comments about it being an "addiction" that we "can't help ourselves but to play" feels a bit like an exaggeration, or an abstraction away from the more simple truth that it's just fun to read so like why not do fun things? Selebus's perfectionism is likely directed more at attempts to pre-emptively slay critics and shore up his self-confidence more than anything (and I so freely make guesses like this since the work invites it), but an undeniable side effect is pristine prose and thoughtful writing which is a pleasure to partake in. Good writing (and through it good character) is just way under-valued despite the enormous effect it has on enjoyment. I saw a completely ridiculous review from someone who said to play the original version of chapter 1 rather than the remade version because it introduced the horror better; this is STAGGERINGLY bad advice because, if for no other reason, the remade version has immensely better writing which improves the experience every single step of the way. So all other things equal I would encourage my past self to start Lessons in Love faster, if anything, to begin partaking in this fruit earlier rather than later.

Something Darker
: Ayane mentioned that she noticed they way Sensei looked at her has changed recently, which prompted her to jump the gun and start actually pursuing what she originally thought would be an impossible wish (
Operation: Fallen Angel
). The same thing might've happened to Ami as well; she started feeling her uncle's gaze becoming scorching after Sensei's reincarnation, which also prompted the incestuous niece to no longer shy away from entrapping her uncle,
someone that
she always wanted anyway
. There is a little dialogue during BREED YOUR NIECE minigame that can sum this up.
Of course, any material from that minigame will have to go through some validation processes so don't take it too seriously; but the point I want to make is that there
are
ways that can rationalize Am's early actions even when I assume she knew absolutely nothing, just like how you would perceive
Something Darker
before the last update arrived (unless it has never made sense to you). Being able to look at early Ami in a different light is one exciting thing, but whether that point of view matches everything else is a different story.

While I always like your stances on anything LiL related, I feel like this is one of the rare cases in which I have doubts or am at least cautious to agree with you yet.

On the multiple Ami topic, the 'Lamb Legs' Happy Event seems to imply that Ami isn't always the Ami we know.

There's likely something else at play:
Ami(?) - "All of this, though?"
- "These hands..."
- "These smiles..."
- "Those aren't me."
- "Those will never be me."
- "And I need you to know that, more than anything else..."
- "Thank you for coming to the special bonus Ami scene."
- "I really have waited forever."

With the likes of Nao taking Ami's form, and possibly her body at times:
Nao - "You may call me a guardian angel if you like, but I prefer the name 'Nao.'"
('Mother's Milk' Happy Event)
Sekai/whatever is Sekai, whispering things in Ami's ear:
Sekai - "All of the above."
Ami - "It's all of the above, obviously."
(Chapter 4 Niki 'That Fuzzy Feeling' Event)
And that Ami Prime thinking Maya is pretending to be her:
Ami Prime (?) - "Because it's one thing to borrow my things, and another to borrow my clothes. But when you're doing both at the same time...you're just pretending to be me."
- "So of course I'm going to get a little weirded out. That's creepy as hell."
(Chapter 4 Maya 'Right As Rain' Event)

There's likely something really convoluted going on when it comes to Ami.

Not to mention, the whole getting murdered and put on display thing:
The Amy at the Pareidolia Mall:
That Twisted Ami thing:
Special Ami:
And Happy Ending Ami:
Etc.

It's likely far too early to draw any concrete conclusions about what's actually going on with Ami.

('Rain King' Happy Event)

Maybe when things really start getting bad, it'll become more clear about how things got to that point.

Ami. Ami?:
Himawari - "But the unfortunate truth is that if you knew who I was, you wouldn't be able to go back at all."
(Chapter 3 Nodoka 'Beyond the Reach of God' Event)

posts.content_html_raw:
Another quick note on the topic of '"Does Ami know more than she alludes to since the beginning?", here's an excerpt from the Chapter 1 Maya event Rewind/Repeat/Refuse.
Foe context: Akira enters Ami's and Maya's dorm room, they sit together and Ami invites him to join but Maya obviously is against it. Ultimately Ami forces them to spend time together by leaving to go take a shower so Akira and Maya talk about why she avoids him and that Akira will keep pursuing to be friends with her.
This is basically how this conversation ends:
Now I think this would be one of the examples that would support Moonflare's theory quite nicely. Assuming Ami is all-knowing to some extent, she might have planned to force those two together so that Akira gets annoyed and stops wanting to spend time with Maya and focus on Ami more.
Except, at the end of the day, as well all know, this does not work. It actually backfires. Maya's resolve seems to crumble, she even seems to realize that this Akira is different than the majority she had to deal with in past cycles. It becomes really obvious here:
In true Prime Maya fashion, she makes it sounds like it's pathetic and dumb of him to do that, yet I am certain that deep inside, she is stoked to find out that this iteration of Akira is not blindly pursuing the first girl that shows him affection (like Ami or Karin from other cycles) but that he is actively trying to befriend the objectively most uninterested and least convenient option out of all of them - her.
The player does not know this at this time, of course. But Ami would know, right? She mentions that Maya is acting weirdly and that Akira is trying to get to know her but that Maya somehow is not interested. Wouldn't an all-knowing Ami be on Maya's side instead of Akira's? What would be her goal in all of this, when her own behavior favors the two of them getting closer together?

I will die on this hill, I believe we are all ultimately victims of confirmation bias and will interpret past interactions to what fits our own views. To me it is not clear whatsoever that Ami has any form of prior knowledge of her own (by that I exclude any God and Sekai involvement). She really does act like a horny teenage girl that is really into her uncle and wants what's best for her friends. At least at the beginning of the game.

Edit:
Bonus Yumi scene, because we all love her.

Key, you say? *looks at previews for the new update* Also Nodoka saying to not go to the roof...

As I said, there is tons of hints and foreboding phrasing in the early game, Sel is a cheeky lil guy. That doesn't mean that Yumi knows more than Akira at this point though.

posts.content_html_raw:
There’s nothing wrong with feeling an emotional reaction to something that happens to a character. So long as you remember that it’s just a game at the end of the day, I see it as a very normal thing to do.

I can remember several extreme emotions I’ve had of this game very well…

- “Uhhh, what the fuck is this?” - Me stumbling into The Room With Clocks for the first time.

- Me looking on in horror as Sensei forces himself on Yumi in “This Town Has Two Halves”, with me thinking I somehow picked the wrong choice, when it was inevitable.

- Me watching with bated breath as Sensei blacked out on Molly at Halloween, and wondering how the hell he would get out of this situation once Tsuneyo walked in.

- Me tearfully smiling during “Spotless Mind” when Akira regained his first memory. That was the first blatant moment of the game where we see that Sensei does have a past here, and isn’t just a random dude who got reincarnated in his body. (Also memories.mp3 is such a good fucking song)

- Me wanting to absolutely smack the hell out of Nodoka for what she put Yumi through in the locker room.

- Me wanting to do the same to Otoha for how she treated Rin and straight up kissed Niki without warning.

- That entire Niki chain in 0.29, especially “The End of the Tour (Glasswalker)” was masterful and made me feel all sorts of ways.

- “I Will Deliver You to the Fireflies”. Come on…

- “Stomachache” deserves mentioning. By far the most disturbing event in this game to date. I had to stand up and walk around for a few minutes afterwards to process what I had just read. It was definitely icky.

- I also got emotional when Maya Prime died, and even worse, that was the newest version of the game at the time I started playing. That cliffhanger was a rough one…

When you tell a story, especially one rich in characterization, your goal is to get the player to connect with your characters. And the connection is precisely what makes some of the drama and ‘holy shit’ moments all the more impactful.

Take Arthur Morgan for example. To anyone who has played this game, you already know where I’m going with this.

I don’t cry often, but when Arthur gave up everything he had and died on that mountaintop, I cried real tears.

That’s just how powerful storytelling can be. That means you did a good job

We all react to things differently, though, and that’s fine.

But yes, LiL is a game that is very much trying to illicit emotional responses out of the player, so it’s perfectly valid if you feel a certain way.

Carbon13 said:
Looks like I'm coming in at the right time with the discussion over whether a VN can be traumatic. I'm putting this one down, probably for good. This is the darkest, most depressing thing I've ever read. I'm not even all the way through Ch.2 and I came on here and the wiki to see if things get better, and no. No they do not.

But that leads me to a question: to all of you who enjoy this, why? Genuine question, not a dig. What is it you get out of this? I'm genuinely curious as to what you DO feel reading these things. If anyone wants to weigh in, please do.

I just needed to get some thoughts out and now I'm going to go interact with the real world, which is shockingly not as dark as this VN, at least not as constantly. And that's not a sentence I ever thought I'd say.
Click to expand...
You shouldn't feel bad about this not being for you, this is highly traumatic content because it deals with trauma in a rather visceral way. Not everyone would be able to deal with it, or even have a reason to expose themselves to it.

Because of the subject matter, it would be expected that a substancial amount of people here have experienced trauma enough in their lives that they can relate to what is portrayed in the game in some form or another, and that's one of reasons as to why they're here. Would it be as traumatic for them (that have experienced these things in real life) as to someone that is experiencing them in a "safe" manner through a videogame with made up characters? I guess that could go either way. I remember a very distant time in my life where realising that partners cheated on one another was traumatic. Trauma can mean a lot of stuff, having to deal with a shade of the world that you didn't realise existed, or at least hadn't confronted in such a clear cut way, can certainly be distressing.

Trauma talk out of the way, "adult" games and media (especially underground media) has a rare opportunity to talk about stuff that you'll rarely find anywhere else. Lessons in Love, in that sense, is a rare product in that Selebus deals with very raw and disgusting aspects of real life holding back nothing. Pedophilia and grooming are its main themes, even though there are so many others, and you'll be able to have productive discussions about all of them after the events, which we have on the regular. Other than that, the narrative, especially the character arcs are compelling, and we work as a community to solve the hints about the overall and supernatural narrative.

Again, if it's not for you, it's not for you. Rather, I'd imagine it's not for most people.
